docs.title: Zeta-80 a Z80 ROMless SBC
docs.text: Repository: github.com/gloveboxes/Z80ROMlessSBC

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
This breadboard design has been proven to drive the Z80 at its maximum clock speed of 20 MHz. It pairs a Z80 processor with a Raspberry Pi Pico 2 W to run CP/M without a ROM chip.

The Z80 runs from 64 KiB of SRAM. The Pico handles clocking, boot loading and verification, and terminal and disk I/O, with scope for true random number generation, timers, and internet access. Four persistent CP/M drives live in the Pico's onboard flash. Phase 9 uses a USB terminal; Phase 10 adds a browser-based WebSocket terminal. After bring-up, the Phase 9 automatic loader starts CP/M on Pico reset, ready for a later picocom connection.

This guide covers the hardware, firmware, and phased tests needed to reproduce the build. Validate your own wiring and operation as you go; clock-rate qualification and timing margins require measurements on your build.

docs.title: Start building
docs.text:
Install the software listed in Toolchain, including the complete Arm compiler, Python, Pico SDK and USB utilities.

  1. Check the parts inventory and read the breadboard and meter basics.
  2. Follow the implementation plan in order, from power checks through SRAM loading, CP/M, and terminal and disk testing.
  3. Use the firmware build and flashing guide to build and load the firmware for your current phase.

The hardware chapters are detailed references; you do not need to understand every firmware excerpt before starting. Use the glossary for unfamiliar terms.

docs.title: How does it boot without ROM?
docs.text:
The Pico feeds the Z80 instructions that make it write and verify its own boot image in SRAM. After verification, the Z80 is reset and starts executing that image from RAM. The Pico never drives the memory address bus or writes SRAM directly.

See the loader sequence for the protocol and timing, and Phase 6 for the implementation and hardware checks.

docs.title: System architecture
docs.text:
The Pico 2 W is a multicore I/O controller: core 0 generates the nominal 20 MHz Z80 clock and owns assisted SRAM loading and Z80 I/O; core 1 owns USB, runtime storage, Wi-Fi and network clients. Bounded console rings and request/result mailboxes separate the two cores. The Z80 itself writes SRAM during loading and executes CP/M directly from SRAM after verification and reset. USB supervisor commands request Z80 actions through a bounded queue; USB interrupts and endpoint operations remain on core 1.

Open or download the full-size SVG. The diagram follows the maintained Phase 10 implementation, which compiles the Phase 9 automatic-loader application with networking enabled.

docs.title: Working and tested breadboard implementation
docs.text:
The breadboard implementation shown below has been built and tested, running the Z80 at 20 MHz with CP/M executing from SRAM. It brings together the Z80, Pico 2 W, SRAM, and interface logic across three BB830 breadboards.

Follow the staged implementation plan to reproduce the build and validate each stage, from power and clock checks through ROMless boot loading, terminal access, and persistent disk I/O.

docs.title: Explore further
docs.text:
• USB CP/M terminal and flash storage - load CP/M, reach the prompt, and test persistent disk I/O.
  • System operation - virtual I/O, flash storage, and runtime coordination.
  • I/O ports and services - the terminal and disk interface, plus ROMLESS-SVC/1 timers, clock, utilities and persistent environment variables.
  • CP/M documentation - boot-image construction, disk media, and software compatibility.
  • Firmware testing - host tests, Z80 emulation, and hardware validation boundaries.
  • Pico flashing and USB supervisor tools - environment setup, verified firmware and selective disk updates, serial discovery, clean stop, and journal diagnostics.
  • Source index - maintained firmware, tools, and implementation guides.

docs.title: Related projects
docs.text:
Two related projects provide a C development toolchain and a collection of CP/M applications and disk images for this computer. Together, they offer a path from C source on a modern development machine to applications running under CP/M on this project's real Z80.

C Compiler & toolchain DCC C Compiler Build C applications on your computer. Run them on a Z80 under CP/M. Explore DCC ↗ 8800 Applications & disk images Altair 8800 AI Edition Explore CP/M applications and build disk images for this Z80 computer. Explore Altair ↗

The disks supplied with this project already include a default set of applications. The system boots 64K CP/M 2.2 - Burcon Z80 Edition, a custom version of the original Burcon CP/M 2.2 and BIOS, modified and optimised for the Z80 and this board. You can use these supplied disks when you reach the CP/M phases; building or importing additional applications is optional.

This is the application-development goal for the later stages of the project. Start with the staged hardware bring-up, completing the documented electrical checks and tests in Phases 0–8 before proceeding to CP/M disk deployment. Those phases establish correct power, clock, bus, SRAM, and I/O operation on your board.

Phase 9 introduces flash-backed disks, Z80 CP/M booting, and applications through the USB terminal. Phase 10 adds the WebSocket terminal. The deployment example below describes the completed Phase 10 system; follow each phase's own firmware and validation instructions as you reach it.

docs.title: DCC C Compiler
docs.text:
The DCC C Compiler builds Z80 CP/M .COM applications on Windows, macOS, and Linux. It supports C89 with selected C99/C11 features, making it possible to write C applications with modern development tools for a CP/M target. Its documentation includes a C conformance guide describing supported features and target exceptions.

DCC translates C source into M80 assembly, then uses M80 and L80 to assemble and link the executable. Its dccmake command coordinates the build, and its runtime provides console and file I/O and other C library facilities suited to CP/M. See this project's CP/M and DCC compatibility overview for the runtime environment provided by the Z80 ROMless SBC.

docs.title: Altair 8800 AI Edition
docs.text:
Altair 8800 AI Edition includes a collection of CP/M/Z80 applications in its Apps folder. The collection includes C applications built with DCC and tooling to package applications into Altair 88-DCDD disk images. These images can also supply applications for the Z80 ROMless SBC.

Once the earlier bring-up tests pass and you reach Phases 9–10, use the following workflow to bring applications across from the Altair project.

docs.title: In the ESP32 Altair 8800 AI Edition project
docs.text:
1. Build the desired C application in the Altair project's Apps collection using its DCC build instructions, and create the corresponding 88-DCDD .dsk image.
  2. Find the source disk images in the Altair project's /esp32-altair-8800/disks folder, then copy the desired .dsk image into Z80ROMlessSBC/src/disks/source-altair/.

docs.title: In the Z80ROMlessSBC project
docs.text:
These steps target the completed Phase 10 hardware and firmware setup. When first bringing up Phase 9, use its USB CP/M and flash storage instructions and complete its tests before moving on to Phase 10.

  1. Open the Z80ROMlessSBC project folder in VS Code. Choose Terminal → Run Task and select one of the disk deployment tasks listed below. The task automatically prepares the copied disk images and installs them into the Pico's flash storage.
  2. After deploying the disks, choose Terminal → Run Task → Build and flash Pico - Phase 10 firmware to build and deploy the Pico firmware for the Z80 boot process. This task preserves the disks you just installed.
  3. With both the disks and Pico firmware deployed, boot CP/M on the real Z80 and access the installed applications on the configured drives A: through D:.

The Pico serves the flash-backed disks while the Z80 executes CP/M and its applications. Disk conversion and provisioning are handled by the dedicated VS Code disk deployment tasks; no manual conversion commands are required. See the disk provisioning details for how this works. The firmware uses native 327,680-byte images rather than the original 88-DCDD sector framing.

docs.title: VS Code disk deployment tasks
docs.text:
The tasks in .vscode/tasks.json use the following source images from src/disks/source-altair/:

Task Disks replaced Source image Flash Pico - All disks (A-D) A: through D: All four images listed below Flash Pico - Drive A A: cpm63k.dsk Flash Pico - Drive B B: bdsc-v1.60.dsk Flash Pico - Drive C C: escape-posix.dsk Flash Pico - Drive D D: blank.dsk

Copy an updated disk image using the filename expected by its task, or update the task's source path to select a different application image. The A: tasks regenerate the board-native boot disk; the B:–D: tasks convert the selected Altair images at flash time. The tasks replace the selected disks without backups and preserve firmware, the installed boot package, and ENV settings. Follow the task's confirmation prompt before deployment.

Drive A: also contains the boot system and needs the board-native BIOS and matching boot package. Drives B: through D: can hold application disks converted from validated Altair images. See Phase 9: USB CP/M and flash storage for the storage design and the disk media README for conversion commands, the default source-image mapping, and selective installation of application disks.

docs.title: Toolchain
docs.text:
Install these tools before building the Pico firmware. The Arm compiler builds the Pico application; a separate Z80 assembler builds the programs that run on the Z80. Python runs the build helpers, embeds the browser terminal in firmware, and prepares CP/M disk images.

Run project commands from the repository root. The checked-in VS Code tasks use macOS/Linux shell syntax. Native Windows setup and its current limitations are described below.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
Tool Used for When required Git Checkout, Pico SDK and recursive submodules All firmware builds Complete Arm GNU Toolchain (arm-none-eabi) Pico C/C++ compilation, linking and binary utilities; includes Newlib and the C++ runtime All firmware builds CMake and Ninja Configure and build the firmware All firmware builds Native C/C++ compiler Build host tools such as pioasm; run native firmware tests SDK tools and host tests Python 3.11 or newer, with pip and venv Build scripts, embedded HTML, CP/M image generation and USB utilities All firmware builds Raspberry Pi Pico SDK, including submodules RP2350, USB and Pico 2 W Wi-Fi libraries All firmware builds picotool Generate RP2350 firmware outputs and program/verify the Pico over USB Firmware builds and flashing z80asm Assemble Z80 diagnostics, BIOS, CCP/BDOS and AUTORUN Top-level firmware CMake configuration, Phase 6 scope/soak targets and CP/M images z80dasm Independent Z80 binary disassembly and assembly/disassembly checks Optional inspection and CP/M audit work Bundled disassemble_cpm64.py Disassemble/audit the preserved CP/M image and generate its Z80 source port CP/M source regeneration/audit; Python standard library only cpmtools (cpmcp, cpmrm) Install native CP/M programs into disk images CP/M image generation picocom, or a Windows serial terminal USB console and supervisor commands Hardware bring-up and USB console use pyserial Discover and communicate with USB serial devices from Python Project USB utilities lsof and ps Check serial ownership and release picocom before flashing Project flash/supervisor scripts on macOS/Linux VS Code Editor and convenient build/flash tasks Optional MkDocs and the project's documentation packages Build or preview this website Documentation work only

picotool is Raspberry Pi's device/binary utility. picocom is a serial terminal. They serve different purposes; installing one does not install the other. The utility's command is picotool, singular.

docs.title: macOS
docs.text:
Install Apple's Command Line Tools if absent, then install the host packages using Homebrew:

xcode-select --install
brew install git cmake ninja python picotool picocom z80asm cpmtools

The Command Line Tools supply the native Clang compiler and developer tools. Install the complete Arm compiler separately using the next section. The Homebrew arm-none-eabi-gcc formula alone lacks the Newlib runtime required by this project; the project has encountered missing -lc and -lg link errors with that installation.

docs.title: Linux (Debian/Ubuntu)
docs.text:
Install the host tools and USB development library:

sudo apt update
sudo apt install build-essential git cmake ninja-build python3 python3-venv \
  python3-pip picocom z80asm cpmtools lsof pkg-config libusb-1.0-0-dev

Check python3 --version is at least 3.11. Install the complete Arm toolchain below, then install a current RP2350-capable picotool from Raspberry Pi's prebuilt SDK tools, or follow its source build instructions. Put the directory containing picotool on PATH. Follow those instructions for Linux USB permissions/udev rules as well; serial access may also require your distribution's serial-device group membership.

docs.title: Windows
docs.text:
Install Git for Windows, CMake, Ninja, and the complete Arm toolchain described below. Enable the installers' PATH options, or add the directories containing their executables to your user Path. Install a native C/C++ build environment, such as Visual Studio Build Tools with its C++ desktop workload, for SDK host tools. Use its Developer PowerShell when those tools need the native compiler.

Windows needs a Python installation in addition to the Arm compiler. Install the Python install manager from Python.org, then install a runtime and check it in a new PowerShell window. The example uses Python 3.14; the project requires 3.11 or newer:

py install 3.14
py -3.14 --version
py -3.14 -m pip --version

For an existing Python installation, py -3 --version and py -3 -m pip --version check the selected interpreter. Follow the official Windows Python guide if py or python is not found; reopen VS Code after changing Path.

Install picotool from Raspberry Pi's SDK tools releases. Make picotool.exe and its supplied runtime dependencies available together, and follow the picotool documentation for Windows USB driver setup. Use a Windows serial terminal such as PuTTY for the Pico's COM port; picocom is used in the macOS/Linux examples.

The checked-in flash tasks and pico_flash.py/pico_supervisor.py workflows currently depend on POSIX shell commands, lsof and ps. Installing Python does not make those workflows native Windows compatible. The automatic toolchain checks in pico_build.py also currently use Unix executable names. With a compatible z80asm also available on PATH, use direct CMake commands for native Windows firmware builds, and the manual BOOTSEL/UF2 procedure for initial programming. Use a Linux environment for the documented z80asm/cpmtools CP/M image workflow; USB access from a virtual Linux environment needs separate configuration.

docs.title: Z80 assembly and disassembly tools
docs.text:
The project's external assembler is NonGNU z80asm. The tested installation reports Z80 assembler version 1.8. build_images.py invokes it with z80asm -o <binary> <source>; CMake also invokes it for the Phase 6 scope/soak and Phase 9/10 disk-diagnostic programs. The checked-in source uses this assembler's syntax and directives. Other assemblers, including the separate z88dk assembler, should not be substituted solely because their executable names look similar.

The top-level CMake project includes the Phase 9/10 definitions during configuration. Their disk-diagnostic generation requires z80asm, so install it before configuring even when your selected build target is an earlier phase. cpmtools is additionally required when generating CP/M disk images.

z80dasm is an optional independent Z80 disassembler, used for the disassembly/assembly round-trip check recorded in the CP/M audit. The current firmware build and Python image scripts do not invoke it automatically. Add it when inspecting binaries or repeating those independent checks:

# macOS
brew install z80asm z80dasm

# Debian/Ubuntu
sudo apt install z80asm z80dasm

Check the installed tools:

z80asm --version
z80dasm --help

The repository also includes src/cpm/disassemble_cpm64.py. This Python tool decodes the preserved Burcon CP/M image, emits an Intel 8080 listing and a Z80 source port, and generates the audit report. It uses Python's standard library and does not require a disassembler package from pip or the z80dasm executable. Its default outputs are checked-in source/report files; pass output paths when generating a separate review copy. Inspect its options with:

python3 src/cpm/disassemble_cpm64.py --help

The arm-none-eabi-objdump and arm-none-eabi-objcopy utilities are supplied with the Arm toolchain. Pico SDK builds use them to produce listings and binary outputs for the Pico firmware. Use z80dasm for inspecting Z80 code.

docs.title: Install the complete Arm GNU toolchain
docs.text:
Use the official Arm GNU Toolchain releases and Arm's installation guide. Select the arm-none-eabi bare-metal target, with both C and C++ support. Match the download's host to the computer doing the build:

Build computer Host package to select Target Apple Silicon Mac darwin-arm64 arm-none-eabi Intel Mac darwin-x86_64 arm-none-eabi Linux PC x86_64 Linux arm-none-eabi 64-bit Linux on Raspberry Pi/Arm aarch64 Linux arm-none-eabi Windows PC Windows installer/archive for the supported host architecture arm-none-eabi

The host architecture does not change the target: the Pico 2 W build uses RP2350 Arm Cortex-M33 code. Select arm-none-eabi rather than the Linux-target or AArch64-target toolchains. Arm GNU Toolchain 15.3.Rel1 / GCC 15.3.1 has passed the project's Phase 6 and Phase 10 builds; the VS Code tasks do not pin that release.

docs.title: macOS and Linux archive installation
docs.text:
1. Download the matching .tar.xz archive from the release page.
  2. Extract it into an empty toolchain directory. The example below uses a stable directory name so your shell configuration need not contain a release number.
  3. Add its bin directory to PATH and verify the runtime libraries.

Replace the archive path with the actual downloaded filename:

arm_archive="$HOME/Downloads/arm-gnu-toolchain-RELEASE-HOST-arm-none-eabi.tar.xz"
arm_install="$HOME/.local/share/arm-gnu-toolchain"
mkdir -p "$arm_install"
tar -xJf "$arm_archive" -C "$arm_install" --strip-components=1
export PATH="$arm_install/bin:$PATH"

Use a fresh directory when installing a different release to avoid mixing toolchains. A versioned name such as arm-gnu-toolchain-<release> also works. To keep the example installation on PATH, add this line to ~/.zshrc on macOS or your Linux shell's startup file, then open a new terminal:

export PATH="$HOME/.local/share/arm-gnu-toolchain/bin:$PATH"

The macOS .pkg installer is an alternative. If you use it, add its installed bin directory to PATH; it may be under /Applications/ArmGNUToolchain/.

docs.title: Windows installer or ZIP installation
docs.text:
Run Arm's Windows installer, or extract the Windows ZIP archive into a chosen directory. Keep the entire directory tree, including the libraries beside bin. Add the directory containing arm-none-eabi-gcc.exe to your user Path, then open a new PowerShell window. For a temporary session, replace the example below with the actual installation directory:

$armBin = 'C:\Tools\ArmGNUToolchain\bin'
$env:Path = "$armBin;$env:Path"

docs.title: Verify the compiler and runtimes
docs.text:
Run these checks after updating PATH; the same commands work in PowerShell:

arm-none-eabi-gcc --version
arm-none-eabi-g++ --version
arm-none-eabi-gcc -mcpu=cortex-m33 -mthumb -mfloat-abi=softfp -print-file-name=libc.a
arm-none-eabi-gcc -mcpu=cortex-m33 -mthumb -mfloat-abi=softfp -print-file-name=libg.a
arm-none-eabi-g++ -mcpu=cortex-m33 -mthumb -mfloat-abi=softfp -print-file-name=libstdc++.a

The last three commands must print paths to installed library files. An output of just libc.a, libg.a or libstdc++.a means the selected compiler cannot find that runtime. Check which compiler is selected with command -v arm-none-eabi-gcc on macOS/Linux, or Get-Command arm-none-eabi-gcc in PowerShell.

docs.title: Checkout and Pico SDK
docs.text:
Clone the project and its WebSocket library submodule:

git clone --recurse-submodules https://github.com/gloveboxes/Z80ROMlessSBC.git
cd Z80ROMlessSBC

For an existing checkout, use git submodule update --init --recursive. Install a complete Pico SDK, including its submodules, if one is not already installed. For macOS/Linux:

mkdir -p "$HOME/GitHub/pico"
git clone --recurse-submodules https://github.com/raspberrypi/pico-sdk.git \
  "$HOME/GitHub/pico/pico-sdk"
cmake -S . -B build -G Ninja -DPICO_BOARD=pico2_w \
  -DPICO_SDK_PATH="$HOME/GitHub/pico/pico-sdk"

For native Windows, run the equivalent from the project root in PowerShell:

git clone --recurse-submodules https://github.com/raspberrypi/pico-sdk.git "$env:USERPROFILE\GitHub\pico\pico-sdk"
cmake -S . -B build -G Ninja -DPICO_BOARD=pico2_w "-DPICO_SDK_PATH=$env:USERPROFILE\GitHub\pico\pico-sdk"

Reuse an existing SDK by passing its directory to -DPICO_SDK_PATH; the repository's default path belongs to the author's machine. Configure with your own path explicitly. For example, build the first-phase firmware with:

cmake --build build --target z80_stage01_supervisor -j

Choose the target matching your hardware's current phase using the firmware target table.

docs.title: Python packages and USB console
docs.text:
Create a separate Python environment for the project USB utilities. On macOS/Linux, run:

python3 -m venv .venv-flash
.venv-flash/bin/python -m pip install -r scripts/requirements-flash.txt
.venv-flash/bin/python -c 'import sys, serial; print(sys.executable)'

The dependency is pyserial; its Python import name is serial. The VS Code flash tasks activate this environment. Native Windows uses a different environment layout; for Python dependencies and serial-library checks:

py -3 -m venv .venv-flash
.\.venv-flash\Scripts\python.exe -m pip install -r scripts/requirements-flash.txt
.\.venv-flash\Scripts\python.exe -c "import sys, serial; print(sys.executable)"

For a USB terminal, select 115200 baud, 8 data bits, no parity, one stop bit and no flow control. Identify the Pico's actual serial port first. A macOS example is:

picocom --baud 115200 --databits 8 --parity n --stopbits 1 --flow n /dev/cu.usbmodemXXXX

Linux commonly uses /dev/ttyACM0; Windows uses a COM port. Replace these examples with your discovered port. Exit picocom with Ctrl+A, then Ctrl+X. See USB console setup and the Pico utilities guide for device discovery, flashing and the board's required power sequence.

docs.title: VS Code builds and final checks
docs.text:
On macOS/Linux, choose Terminal → Run Task → Build and flash Pico - Phase 10 firmware to build and deploy Phase 10 firmware while preserving disks and ENV. This task uses scripts/pico_build.py for their build step. It searches an explicit ARM_GNU_TOOLCHAIN_BIN override, the build's cached compiler, complete toolchains on PATH, then ~/.local/share/arm-gnu-toolchain*/bin. It checks the runtimes before building. For an installation outside these locations, set the override before starting VS Code, for example:

export ARM_GNU_TOOLCHAIN_BIN="$HOME/.local/share/arm-gnu-toolchain/bin"

An existing CMake build keeps its selected compiler. Use a new build directory when switching toolchains. An explicit cmake --fresh configure also resets the cache; pass your SDK path and keep the desired compiler first on PATH.

Check the host tools without a Pico attached:

git --version
cmake --version
ninja --version
picotool version

Also check z80asm --version before configuring firmware. For CP/M image generation, check that cpmcp and cpmrm are available. For independent binary inspection, check the optional z80dasm --help (its header includes the version). No attached Pico is needed to build firmware.

Continue with firmware build and provisioning, firmware testing, or building the documentation. Documentation dependencies are listed separately in docs/docs/requirements.txt.

docs.title: Appendix D: CP/M BIOS and dcc Compatibility
docs.text:
For a first hardware build, this section is supporting software reference, not a prerequisite for wiring. You can use the interactive host emulator to become familiar with CP/M before the boards are ready. It tests the software path without powering a Pico; it does not qualify the physical buses, flash recovery, or timing.

This system runs CP/M 2.2 with a custom BIOS designed specifically for this board. The image builder packages the 64K CP/M CCP and BDOS with the native BIOS assembled from src/cpm/z80_bios.asm. The BIOS is the layer that translates standard CP/M console and disk operations into this board's Pico-serviced virtual I/O ports. Applications do not need to know that the terminal is a WebSocket or that disk records reside in Pico flash.

dcc targets CP/M 2.2 on the Z80 and emits ordinary .COM programs linked with its Z80 runtime. That execution model is compatible with this system: the dcc runtime enters CP/M through the standard page-zero vectors, CP/M BDOS performs console and file-system policy, and the custom BIOS performs the final hardware-dependent transfer.

docs.title: In this section
docs.text:
For the compiler, C library, and CP/M APIs, see the DCC documentation.

  • Image provenance and machine boundary
  • CP/M memory map and entry points
  • Custom BIOS responsibilities
  • Compatibility boundaries
  • Validation requirements
  • Automated end-to-end test
  • Interactive CP/M test

docs.title: D.3 Custom BIOS Responsibilities
docs.text:
The BIOS supplies the standard CP/M 2.2 jump table expected by BDOS and by dcc's optional direct-BIOS functions. Its principal mappings are:

CP/M BIOS operation Board implementation BOOT Initialize CP/M state and page-zero vectors, then enter the CCP WBOOT Flush pending writes, reload CCP/BDOS from Drive A, and re-enter the CCP CONST Read terminal status port 0x01; return 0xFF when bit 0 reports input ready CONIN Wait for receive-ready, then read terminal data port 0x00 CONOUT Wait for transmit-room bit 1, then write the character to port 0x00 READER Return CP/M text EOF (0x1A); no reader device is implemented LIST / PUNCH Discard output; printer and punch devices are intentionally not implemented LISTST Return not ready because no list device exists SELDSK Validate drives A-D and return the corresponding disk parameter header SETTRK / SETSEC / SETDMA Record the logical disk location and software transfer-buffer address in SRAM; no Pico hardware DMA READ / WRITE Convert track and sector to a linear 128-byte LBA, transfer through ports 0x10-0x14, and preserve CP/M write-type semantics for flash caching SECTRAN Return the sector unchanged because native disk images use linear sector order

CP/M BDOS remains responsible for filenames, FCBs, directory searches, allocation, sequential/random record selection, and text-file conventions. The BIOS sees only drive selection and 128-byte logical records. Consequently, dcc file APIs do not require a board-specific runtime backend: their BDOS file calls eventually reach the custom READ and WRITE entries.

Console ports occupy the aligned 0x00 group and disk ports the aligned 0x10 group. The supervisor samples only A0/A1/A2/A4, equivalent to port & 0x17, so these established addresses remain distinct. A3, A5-A7, and the high I/O address byte alias; see the I/O port map. Every I/O cycle uses the same trap, so moving the canonical ports would not reduce Pico trap work.

docs.title: D.6 Compatibility Boundaries
docs.text:
• Programs must fit within the 0x0100-0xE6FF TPA after runtime, globals, heap, and stack requirements are included.
  • The installed operating system is CP/M 2.2. Optional CP/M 3 or emulator-only BDOS extensions are not supplied by this BIOS/BDOS image. In particular, software should treat dcc's BDOS-105-backed clock functions as unavailable unless separately demonstrated on this target.
  • CP/M filenames and disks retain CP/M 2.2 semantics: 8.3 names, FCB-based access, 128-byte logical records, and Ctrl-Z text-file conventions where the dcc API documents them.
  • The terminal data port returns 0x00 if read while empty. Correct software must test status bit 0 first; BDOS and the custom BIOS already do so.
  • Status bit 7 reports WebSocket client connection state to direct-port software, but CP/M and dcc do not require it for their standard console ABI.
  • dcc's own emulator and physical-Z80 test history establishes general CP/M runtime portability, but it does not by itself qualify this board's Pico trap, custom BIOS, flash backend, or electrical timing.

docs.title: D.8 End-to-End Z80 Optimization, Image Build, and Flash Test
docs.text:
The active bootable system is Z80-optimized throughout its resident software: the CCP and BDOS are emitted as cpm64_z80.asm, and the board BIOS is implemented by z80_bios.asm. The immutable cpm64_system.bin is retained as the fingerprinted Burcon reference and as the input to the translation audit; it is not copied directly into the deployed image. The optimized CCP/BDOS port uses Z80 relative branches, guarded DJNZ, block moves, native arithmetic, tail transfers, and safe register-use rewrites. The BIOS uses the Z80 instruction set for its jump table, cold/warm boot paths, console polling, and disk transfers, including INIR/OTIR, SBC, relative branches, and EXX. The resulting image keeps the CP/M ABI and fixed resident boundaries while leaving the transient program area at 0x0100-0xE6FF.

Build the complete CP/M artifact set from the repository root:

python3 src/cpm/build_images.py --output-dir build/cpm

The builder assembles the optimized CCP/BDOS and BIOS, constructs the reset-ready 64 KiB z80boot.img, wraps it as z80boot.pkg with a manifest and CRC, and replaces only Drive A's reserved system tracks in drive_a_cpm63k-z80.img. Drives B-D remain the converted native 320 KiB images. With a Phase 10 firmware binary, the same builder can compose z80romless-flash.bin, a complete 4 MiB image:

python3 src/cpm/build_images.py --output-dir build/cpm \
  --firmware build/src/stage10_websocket_terminal/z80_stage10_websocket_terminal.bin

The BIOS and flash backend share one deliberately narrow contract. CP/M passes drive, track, sector, DMA address, and write type to the BIOS; the BIOS converts the request to one 128-byte linear-record transfer through ports 0x10-0x14. The Pico maps those records into the four exact 320 KiB flash slots at 0x2C0000, 0x310000, 0x360000, and 0x3B0000. Normal writes can coalesce in a 4 KiB cache, while directory and warm-boot writes are journaled; the write type is preserved so the Pico can choose the safe persistence path. On cold boot, the Pico holds RESET# LOW while recovering the journal and validating the package. It then releases reset and injects instructions under slow clocks so the Z80 writes and reads back the SRAM image. The Z80 alone drives memory addresses and write strobes; this is not Pico memory mastering. After successful verification, the Pico resets the Z80 to PC zero again and starts normal execution from SRAM. The BIOS then installs the page-zero warm-boot and BDOS vectors. On a later warm boot, the BIOS reloads the 44 CCP/BDOS records (5,632 bytes) from Drive A. This avoids a second storage bus while keeping Z80 disk semantics and Pico flash erase/program operations separate.

Run the reproducibility and structure tests with:

python3 -m unittest discover -s src/cpm -p 'test_*.py' -v

These tests assemble both optimized Z80 components and verify the CP/M 2.2 version byte, resident placement, BIOS jump-table ABI, boot-package header and CRCs, exact 64 KiB and 320 KiB geometries, Drive A system-track replacement, and every flash-region boundary. The end-to-end DCC debug-host test additionally boots the optimized image, observes the CP/M banner and A> prompt, runs DIR, executes LS.COM to its natural exit, confirms BIOS warm reload, selects another drive, loads a multi-extent transient, and copies files across drives. After building the project-owned z80-debug-host, run the end-to-end test with:

python3 src/cpm/test_z80_debug_host.py \
  --host build/cpm/z80_debug_host/z80-debug-host

This is host/emulator evidence, not a claim of completed electrical qualification. Physical proof still requires the Phase 8, Phase 9, and Phase 10 bus, flash fault-injection, power-cycle recovery, and logic-analyzer tests listed in the required qualification and implementation plan.

docs.title: CP/M Image Provenance
docs.text: The system boots 64K CP/M 2.2 - Burcon Z80 Edition: a Z80-optimised port of Burcon CP/M 2.2 with a custom BIOS for this board.

docs.title: Original system
docs.text:
• Source: Burcon CP/M 2.2 for the Altair 88-DCDD controller.
  • Reference image: src/cpm/cpm64_system.bin, the 5,632-byte CCP/BDOS region captured after the matching Burcon MOVCPM 64 and SYSGEN tools produced a bootable system in the Altair emulator.
  • Integrity: The image builder checks its SHA-256 fingerprint. This reference binary is preserved unchanged.
  • Original layout: CCP at 0xE300, BDOS at 0xEB00, and BIOS at 0xF900, with a 0x0700-byte BIOS reservation.

To regenerate the reference, use the matching Burcon utilities and MOVCPM instructions. The generator reports SAVE 38; preserve the BIOS reservation and verify relocated entry vectors.

docs.title: Changes for this board
docs.text:
• Z80 CP/M port: src/cpm/cpm64_z80.asm replaces the original CCP/BDOS at build time. Z80 instruction optimisations reclaim 263 bytes while preserving section sizes; the sections move upward by 0x0400. See the memory map for the running system's layout.
  • Custom BIOS: src/cpm/z80_bios.asm replaces the Altair BIOS and cold loader. It uses the board's Pico-serviced terminal and flash-disk ports, rather than the Altair controller's ports 0x08–0x0A. See Custom BIOS.
  • Validation: The port's unoptimised mode reproduces the reference byte-for-byte. Host tests check relocation and Z80 instructions, plus cold boot, DIR, program loading, and warm boot.
  • Audit details: src/cpm/cpm64_i8080.asm and src/cpm/cpm64_i8080_audit.md record the original disassembly and findings.

For supplied applications, DCC builds, and disk deployment, see Related projects.

docs.title: D.9 Interactive End-to-End CP/M User Test
docs.text:
The repository includes an interactive launcher for manually exercising the same optimized CP/M image, board BIOS, virtual-disk protocol, and native disk images used by the automated DCC test.

Prerequisites are CMake, a C/C++ compiler, Python 3, and z80asm. In VS Code:

  1. Open Run and Debug.
  2. Select Interactive CP/M emulator.
  3. Press Start.
  4. Wait for the banner and A> prompt in the Interactive CP/M emulator terminal.
  5. Type CP/M commands normally. Press Ctrl+] to detach and stop the session.

The pre-launch task builds the DCC-derived z80-debug-host, the complete project-owned adapter in src/cpm/dcc_io_adapter, and the CP/M artifacts in build/cpm. The Interactive CP/M emulator debug configuration always passes that built adapter to z80-debug-host; no optional selection or external Altair checkout is required. The launcher extracts the 64 KiB SRAM payload from z80boot.pkg, starts it through the board BIOS, and attaches Drives A-D from the generated 320 KiB images. A successful start displays:

64K CP/M 2.2 - Burcon Z80 Edition

A>

The following manual sequence exercises progressively more of the deployed software path:

A>DIR
A>LS
A>C:
C>ATTNC11
C>A:PIP D:ATTNC11.COM=C:ATTNC11.COM
C>A:PIP D:ATTN.WTS=C:ATTN.WTS
C>D:
D>DIR
  • DIR proves CCP command handling, BDOS directory access, BIOS record reads, the 0x10-0x14 disk-port protocol, and Drive A filesystem interpretation.
  • LS loads and executes a transient program, exits through page zero, and exercises the BIOS warm-boot reload before returning to A>.
  • C: and ATTNC11 exercise drive selection and multi-extent program loading.
  • The PIP commands exercise cross-drive reads, writes, directory updates, and persistence in the emulator's generated Drive D image.

The dynamic adapter preserves the native SBC disk ports 0x10-0x14, uses the loader-only byte A5h on 0x15 for activation, and mirrors all active ports in the ESP32 Altair port_drivers/io_ports.c dispatcher:

Ports Host-emulated function 21-22 Production HTTP(S) file-transfer driver/parser with native asynchronous curl transport 24-31, 37-39, 41-44 Time and timer requests 24-30 Time and timer input 45, 48, 49, 70 Utility strings and host information 46-47 OpenWeatherMap field request and status 52 DCC-host interrupt timer 60-61 Legacy host-file transfer 71-72 Text-file-backed environment variables 120-124 OpenAI-compatible chat request and response 200 Shared response-buffer input

The host adapter intentionally does not add the altair_local Sense HAT extensions because those ports are absent from the firmware source-of-truth dispatcher. Weather and chat use libcurl when available and explicitly report an unavailable/error state when network support or configuration is absent. No API keys are stored in the repository.

docs.title: Build and run FT locally before deployment
docs.text:
The FT integration test assembles the canonical FT.ASM from the sibling ESP32 Altair project with the real CP/M MAC and LOAD programs. It runs the resulting FT.COM against a temporary local Python HTTP server, then optionally downloads the supplied GitHub BASIC example over HTTPS and executes it in MBASIC. The emulator adapter uses the production http_io.c mailbox/port logic and http_stream.c parser; curl supplies the native asynchronous socket/TLS backend. The firmware's Mbed TLS configuration is checked separately by the native live-transfer test.

From the repository root, with Python 3.10+, cpmtools, z80asm and curl development headers/libraries available:

cmake -S src/cpm/z80_debug_host -B build/cpm/z80_debug_host \
  -DZ80_DEBUG_HOST_BUILD_EXAMPLES=OFF -DBUILD_TESTING=OFF
cmake --build build/cpm/z80_debug_host
cmake -S src/cpm/dcc_io_adapter -B build/cpm/dcc_io_adapter
cmake --build build/cpm/dcc_io_adapter
python3 src/cpm/test_http_ft.py --https

The test assembles Apps/FT/FT.ASM from the sibling ESP32 Altair project with CP/M MAC and LOAD. It converts line endings for MAC input and generates a dedicated disk set in build/cpm-http-ft/images. It checks:

  • MAC/LOAD produce a runnable FT.COM under the board's CP/M and BIOS.
  • FT -GB BINARY.BIN saves all 65,797 bytes, including NULs, followed by the expected CP/M record padding; this crosses multiple file extents.
  • An empty binary file completes, HTTP 404 removes the partial file, and the next transfer succeeds after the error.
  • A small MENU.BAS fixture checks mixed line-ending normalization and lets LOVE's final RUN "MENU" return cleanly to BASIC.
  • Running FT -G without a filename prompts for MiXeD.Bas, requests that exact remote path, and saves its contents as uppercase MIXED.BAS.
  • With --https, FT -G LOVE.BAS downloads all 1,664 source bytes, saves the expected CR LF text and ^Z/record padding, then MBASIC loads and executes it.

The build leaves FT.COM, results.json with source/file hashes, and readable transcript.txt plus debugger transcript.mi in build/cpm-http-ft. The original source and ordinary build/cpm disks are unchanged by this test. No Pico is accessed. Loader activation stays latched until CPU reset; FT commands 1/3/4 on port 21 retain native SBC I/O routing.

Use build_images.cpm_diskdefs() when injecting or extracting native CP/M files with cpmtools. Its reference is the ESP32 Altair project's diskdefs entry altair88, which already explicitly sets logicalextents 1 to match the Burcon BIOS's EXM=0. This board's native definition uses 80 tracks and skew 1 because conversion has already applied the Altair sector mapping. The other shared filesystem parameters come from src/disks/geometry.py. Keep the explicit logical-extent setting: inferring extents from the 2 KiB block size produces incompatible files larger than 16 KiB. The test explicitly flushes the modeled disk before reading saved files from another process.

Terminal input uses the same policy as altair_local: Up/Down/Right/Left map to Ctrl-E/Ctrl-X/Ctrl-D/Ctrl-S, Insert/Delete map to Ctrl-O/Ctrl-G, Page Up/Page Down map to Ctrl-R/Ctrl-V, and Backspace or Delete maps to Ctrl-H. A standalone Escape is emitted after a 30 ms grace period, allowing ANSI cursor sequences to be recognized without losing Escape as a CP/M command key.

This is a realistic end-to-end software-path test: it executes the optimized CCP/BDOS and z80_bios.asm with the SRAM payload extracted from the packaged boot artifact, while the BIOS accesses the same native disk-image format that is provisioned into Pico flash. Disk writes are made to the generated files under build/cpm; rerunning the preparation task regenerates those artifacts, so copy out any test result that must be retained.

The launcher intentionally substitutes host files for the physical Pico flash backend. It therefore does not validate Pico package/CRC handling, the physical flash cache and journal implementation, power-loss recovery, the Pico-to-SRAM injected loading, WAIT#/bus timing, voltage translation, or the assembled board. Those remain Phase 8, Phase 9, and Phase 10 hardware and firmware qualification items.

docs.title: D.2 CP/M Memory Map and Entry Points
docs.text:
The reset-ready SRAM image uses the following upper-memory layout:

Region Address range Role Page zero 0x0000-0x00FF CP/M vectors, default FCBs, DMA buffer, and command tail Transient Program Area (TPA) 0x0100-0xE6FF .COM program, dcc runtime, static data, heap, and stack CCP 0xE700-0xEEFF Console Command Processor, reloaded after a warm boot BDOS 0xEF00-0xFCFF CP/M console, file, and disk service layer; entry at 0xEF06 BIOS 0xFD00-0xFFCD 718-byte Z80-optimized boot, console, disk, translation and startup-report routines

The TPA contains 0xE600 bytes, or 58,880 bytes, before the CCP boundary. A dcc program and every runtime block selected for it must fit in this space together with its stack and heap. The dcc runtime reads the installed JP 0xEF06 vector at 0x0005 to locate BDOS; application memory must still remain below the CCP boundary at 0xE700. Required CCP/BDOS workspace, the BIOS directory buffer and allocation vectors, disk state, and internal stacks remain inside their relocated resident regions.

The BIOS cold boot installs JP instructions at 0x0000 and 0x0005 for warm boot and BDOS respectively. A dcc program normally starts at 0x0100 and returns to CP/M through the warm-boot vector. Because a transient program may overwrite the resident CCP while using the TPA, the custom warm boot reloads the 44 CCP/BDOS system records before returning to the command prompt.

docs.title: D.7 Validation Status and Required Qualification
docs.text:
The host regression suite assembles the custom BIOS and verifies its placement, the CCP/BDOS fingerprint, page-zero reset target, boot-package headers and CRCs, native disk construction, CP/M geometry, and complete 4 MiB flash layout. These are structural and reproducibility checks; they do not execute dcc programs through this BIOS or measure a physical I/O cycle.

Separately, the source Burcon system has been cold-booted in the Altair host emulator as 64K CP/M, reached the A> prompt, and completed DIR. That test validates the relocated CCP/BDOS artifact and Burcon memory ABI, but it executes the Altair BIOS rather than this board's custom BIOS. It therefore does not validate the Pico I/O trap, virtual terminal and disk ports, flash persistence, or Z80 bus timing.

The design remains unvalidated in hardware as stated in the Overview. Before claiming dcc compatibility on the completed machine, perform Phase 8, Phase 9, and Phase 10, then run representative dcc .COM programs that cover:

  1. printf/puts, literal $, CR/LF conversion, buffering, and fflush.
  2. getchar, scanf, kbhit, getch, Ctrl-Z, and browser reconnect behavior.
  3. File create, close, reopen, sequential read/write, random access, rename, delete, directory updates, disk-full handling, and warm boot.
  4. Transfers on drives A-D, including repeated writes followed by power-cycle recovery and byte-for-byte host comparison.
  5. A dcc program near the TPA limit, confirming that stack/heap growth does not cross 0xE700 and that exit reliably reloads the CCP.

Passing those application tests, the existing all-LBA and fault-injection disk plan, and the logic-analyzer requirements is the point at which console and file-I/O compatibility may be described as proven on this hardware.

docs.title: Building the documentation
docs.text: The MkDocs source lives in docs/docs/en, with navigation in docs/docs/mkdocs.yml. It is the single source of truth for the complete engineering specification; do not recreate a monolithic copy in the project README.

docs.title: Build the website
docs.text:
From docs/docs, create an environment, install the documentation dependencies, and run a strict build:

python3 -m venv .venv
.venv/bin/python -m pip install -r requirements.txt
.venv/bin/mkdocs build --strict

The generated website is written to docs/site from the repository root.

docs.title: Source-backed phase code
docs.text:
Phase 1-10 use the existing include-markdown plugin's plain include directive inside fenced code blocks and collapsed ??? example sections. Each section includes one complete maintained file from src/; do not paste firmware into Markdown or use line-number slices that drift when code changes. Use include, not include-markdown, for source code so Markdown link and heading transformations do not alter it.

Paths are relative to the phase page. From en/implementation/, the repository source tree is ../../../../src/. Keep the source path in the section title and retain links to related headers and build definitions in the source index.

Every documentation build reads the current checkout. The MkDocs configuration explicitly watches ../../src during mkdocs serve, so source edits continue to trigger preview rebuilds even if the include plugin loses its per-file watches after a rebuild. A published site reflects its last deployed revision, not subsequent local changes. Build from the complete repository so the included sources are available; a missing include is a build error.

docs.title: Deferred PCB documentation
docs.text: The historical PCB pages remain in docs/docs/en/pcb/, but exclude_docs in the MkDocs configuration excludes them from generated pages and search. They are also absent from navigation. Keep them hidden until PCB migration is separately reviewed; do not regenerate the historical PCB or fabrication artifacts as part of a documentation build.

docs.title: Serve locally
docs.text:
.venv/bin/mkdocs serve

MkDocs prints the preview URL, normally http://127.0.0.1:8000/.

docs.title: Deploy
docs.text: .github/workflows/docs.yml performs a strict build and publishes the site to the gh-pages branch whenever main changes. It can also be run manually with the GitHub Actions workflow_dispatch control.

docs.title: Hardware Design
docs.text:
The hardware chapters progress from the bill of materials through pin-level wiring, address generation, physical construction, buffering, and final bus isolation. For a first build, read the inventory and construction basics, then follow the phased implementation plan. Consult the other hardware chapters when a phase refers to them; their chapter order is not the chip-installation order.

Chapter Purpose 0. Project inventory Parts, passive components, power distribution, and required bench equipment 1. Reference pin mapping Authoritative IC pin maps, signal ownership, and logic-domain checks 2. Address interface Z80-assisted loading and four-bit port monitoring 3. Physical construction Breadboard topology, socket placement, and jumper routing 4. Output buffer AHCT244 channel allocation and enable behavior 5. Bus isolation Address, data, and control transceiver operating modes

The historical PCB documentation is hidden while migration is deferred. The existing PCB, BOM, and fabrication files are unchanged and incompatible with this assisted-loader revision. Do not manufacture that package for this build.

The instrument procedures are cross-cutting qualification references rather than additional hardware chapters. Use the RIGOL DHO814 capture plan for analogue integrity and exact timing, and the DSLogic Plus capture plan for bus-wide digital state and event ordering. Individual implementation pass gates name the captures required at each phase.

docs.title: 2. Z80-Assisted Loading and Address Monitoring
docs.text: The Pico never drives A0-A15 and never asserts an SRAM write strobe. The fully static CMOS Z80 executes injected instructions under a slow Pico clock. This removes the address expander, programmable logic, and external programming dependency from the circuit.

docs.title: Loader Sequence
docs.text:
1. Disable both data paths and PWM. Assert RESET# for at least six slow clock cycles, then release it and clock two reset-exit cycles.
  2. Keep BOOT_READ_DISABLE HIGH. SRAM OE# stays HIGH while the Pico supplies opcode and immediate bytes during Z80 read cycles.
  3. Inject LD HL,nn (21 low high), then LD (HL),n (36 byte). Disable the Pico output after the operand read; the Z80 drives the address, data, and write controls for the following three write T-states.
  4. For verification, inject LD A,(HL) (7E), disable the upward path, enable the downward path, and lower BOOT_READ_DISABLE only for the three memory-read T-states. Sample the bus before the last clock; inhibit SRAM reads again afterward.
  5. Compare every byte. On success, reset the Z80 again so PC is zero, isolate both paths, lower BOOT_READ_DISABLE, release RESET# while CLK is stopped LOW, wait at least 1 us, then start the normal clock. On failure, hold RESET# LOW and stop the clock.

Opcode fetches use four T-states; immediate reads use three. Every byte access reloads HL, favoring a simple checked implementation over boot speed. These operations require an initialized loader session and are not runtime DMA. Each slow clock returns with CLK LOW only after a fixed 1 us settling interval. This retains injected data through the Z80's RD# release and lets the buffered controls settle before readback or isolation. The pulse count, not a fixed slow-clock frequency, defines the instruction sequence; software overhead and extra settling extend the low intervals. PWM-to-SIO handover adds a one-time 1 us guard; already-SIO steps do not repeat that guard. An injected step requests 1 us LOW, 1 us HIGH, and 1 us of trailing settling, rather than a fixed 500 kHz clock. At 37 clocks per loaded-and-verified byte, the 64 KiB image requires about 7.27 seconds of clock waits alone; data turnaround waits, instructions, and other overhead increase the real boot time. The host cycle model tests ordering, boundary addresses, patterns, March, and readback errors; actual reset phase and bus timing still require bench captures.

Maintained source: sram.c and cpu.c.

docs.title: Port Address Monitor
docs.text:
U7, a 3.3 V-powered SN74LVC244AN, monitors four address bits and four controls. Tie enables pins 1/19 and GND pin 10 to GND; VCC pin 20 to Pico 3.3 V.

Signal Z80 pin U7 input U7 output Pico GPIO / header BUSACK# 23 2 18 GP0 / 1 IORQ# 20 4 16 GP1 / 2 RD# 21 6 14 GP27 / 32 WR# 22 8 12 GP28 / 34 A0 30 11 9 GP18 / 24 A1 31 13 7 GP19 / 25 A2 32 15 5 GP20 / 26 A4 34 17 3 GP21 / 27 
block-beta
  columns 2
  Z0["Z80 A0 - pin 30"] L0["LVC244 input - pin 11"]
  Z1["Z80 A1 - pin 31"] L1["LVC244 input - pin 13"]
  Z2["Z80 A2 - pin 32"] L2["LVC244 input - pin 15"]
  Z4["Z80 A4 - pin 34"] L4["LVC244 input - pin 17"]
  Z0 --> L0
  Z1 --> L1
  Z2 --> L2
  Z4 --> L4

The decoded port is address & 0x17. Terminal ports 00/01 and disk ports 10-14 remain distinct. A3, A5-A7, and the high address byte are intentionally ignored: for example 08 aliases 00, and 18 aliases 10. Unsupported decoded ports retain the existing application behavior. There is no SPI address sampling or address-driver direction to configure.

BUSREQ#/BUSACK# remains solely a CPU-quiescence handshake for runtime flash writes. A granted bus never authorizes Pico memory address or write driving.

docs.title: 5. Bus Translation and Isolation
docs.text: The Z80 is the sole address-bus driver. Two fixed-direction transceivers separate its 5 V data bus from the Pico. Both must be disabled before changing Pico data GPIO direction or value. Never enable both at once.

docs.title: 5.1 Data Paths
docs.text:
Device Supply DIR pin 1 A pins 2-9 B pins 18-11 OE# pin 19 U9 SN74AHCT245N +5 V at pin 20 +5 V, A to B GP10-GP17 D0-D7 HCT32 pin 8 U10 SN74LVC245AN +3.3 V at pin 20 GND, B to A GP10-GP17 D0-D7 GP7

Both GND pins 10 connect to common GND. Add local 100 nF capacitors. The complete bit table specifies every CPU, SRAM, translator, and Pico data pin.

Mode GP6 upward request GP7 downward OE# Upward path Downward path Isolated / run 1 1 Off Off Injected read / IN reply 0 1 On only while RD# LOW Off SRAM verification / OUT 1 0 Off On

GP6 reaches HCT32 pin 10, raw RD# reaches pin 9, and output pin 8 reaches U9 OE#. GP7 drives U10 OE# directly. Both GPIOs have 10 kOhm pulls to 3.3 V; no 5 V output connects to either. Firmware raises both OEs, preloads data before enabling outputs, or initializes all eight inputs before reception. Before driving, it waits at least 1 us after disabling both paths so U10 has stopped driving the Pico pins before their direction changes to output. This is software-controlled exclusion, not an all-state hardware interlock: forcing GP6 and GP7 LOW together is prohibited.

The RD# gate disables upward drive at read completion. Runtime firmware finishes I/O with slow single clocks, observes IORQ#/RD#/WR# release, disables both paths, waits at least 1 us for isolation, rearms WAIT, and only then resumes PWM. Each slow clock includes at least 1 us of settling after its falling edge; firmware must not poll a still-propagating strobe and accidentally step into the next memory cycle. RD# gating alone would not protect a subsequent memory read if the upward request stayed asserted.

Do not substitute TXS/TXB auto-direction parts, BSS138, or resistor-divider modules for this push-pull multi-load bus. The AHCT245 lacks data-port power-off protection: apply external +5 V before USB and remove USB before +5 V. Disabling its OE does not eliminate its input clamp paths.

docs.title: 5.2 CPU-Only Address Ownership
docs.text: Only the Z80 drives A0-A15; SRAM, pulls, and four input-monitor taps share the trunk. Loading requires the Z80 running under injected instructions, not held in reset. BUSACK is retained for flash quiescence, never Pico DMA.

docs.title: 5.3 SN74LVC244AN 5 V-to-3.3 V Input Buffer
docs.text:
All eight monitor channels are used. Supply U7 pin 20 from Pico 3.3 V; pins 1,10,19 go to GND. Its inputs tolerate 5.5 V and Ioff protects power-off. Never wire raw Z80 outputs directly to Pico GPIOs; GP27/GP28 are not FT pads, and FT tolerance on other pads depends on IOVDD being present.

Signal CPU pin U7 input U7 output Pico GP BUSACK# 23 2 18 0 IORQ# 20 4 16 1 RD# 21 6 14 27 WR# 22 8 12 28 A0 30 11 9 18 A1 31 13 7 19 A2 32 15 5 20 A4 34 17 3 21 
block-beta
  columns 2
  ZB["Z80 BUSACK# - pin 23"] LB["LVC244 input - pin 2"]
  ZI["Z80 IORQ# - pin 20"] LI["LVC244 input - pin 4"]
  ZR["Z80 RD# - pin 21"] LR["LVC244 input - pin 6"]
  ZW["Z80 WR# - pin 22"] LW["LVC244 input - pin 8"]
  ZB --> LB
  ZI --> LI
  ZR --> LR
  ZW --> LW

docs.title: 5.4 Implementation Wiring Index
docs.text:
• Pico connections
  • Fixed logic and output buffer
  • Control and port monitor
  • Data paths
  • SRAM and CPU insertion

docs.title: 3. Construction and Breadboard Topology
docs.text: Build the phase sequence; leave later devices absent until instructed. Every pin map is a top view. Matching schematic net labels mean an electrical connection even without a continuous drawn wire.

docs.title: Before You Wire
docs.text:
On each BB830, A-E at one numbered row are one connection; F-J at that row are a separate connection. The center ravine isolates them. Adjacent numbered rows are not connected. Check power-rail continuity with a meter: stripes do not prove internal continuity or voltage.

Wire one named source pin to one named destination pin, then check continuity at the actual socket contacts and shorts to adjacent contacts. GP2 is Pico header pin 4, not header pin 2. A0-A15 means sixteen independent nets. Strip only enough insulation to seat the jumper, with no exposed bridges.

docs.title: Use the Meter Safely
docs.text: Use resistance/continuity only with external power and USB disconnected and capacitors discharged. Do not discharge capacitors by shorting them. In voltage mode, black COM goes to circuit GND and red goes to the named pin. Measure IC supply contacts, not only the supply entry. Prefer the supply current readout; an ammeter goes in series, never across +5 V and GND. Return its lead to the voltage socket after any current measurement. Attach clips with power off.

docs.title: Board Roles and Placement
docs.text: Place Memory, Core, and Peripheral boards left-to-right with long edges parallel, row 1 at the top, A-E left and F-J right. Do not mirror a board. Keep the AHCT244 next to the Z80 so CLK never crosses a board boundary. Signal-group placement is a routing aid, not a wire-length-matching requirement.

docs.title: 3.1 Package Orientation and Pin 1
docs.text:
Board / device Rows Orientation Pin 1 Opposite corner Memory / HCT32 5-11 Notch up E5 Pin 14 at F5 Memory / SRAM 18-33 Notch up Left pin-row side, row 18 Pin 32 right, row 18 Core / AHCT244 8-17 Notch down F17 Pin 20 E17 Core / Z80 19-38 Notch up Left pin-row side, row 19 Pin 40 right, row 19 Peripheral / Pico 1-20 USB up Header 1 left, row 1 Header 40 right, row 1 Peripheral / LVC244 22-31 Notch up E22 Pin 20 F22 Peripheral / AHCT245 33-42 Notch down F42 Pin 20 E42 Peripheral / LVC245 44-53 Notch down F53 Pin 20 E53

Narrow 7.62 mm DIPs straddle the ravine in E/F. Dry-fit the Z80/SRAM wide 15.24 mm sockets in columns matching their actual pin-row spacing; do not bend them into E/F. Both sides must remain electrically isolated. Reserve Core rows 1-3 for supply-module clearance; if the module needs more, mount it off-board rather than compressing the clock/CPU region.

Memory uses 23 terminal rows for ICs, Core 30, and Peripheral 50. Leave gaps, keep bypass capacitors near supply pins, and place address pulls by the SRAM trunk and Pico data pulls beside U9/U10 A pins. No reset transistor is fitted.

docs.title: Power Distribution
docs.text:
Feed the three +5 V rails from one supply-entry star, with multiple short common-GND links near bus crossings. The Peripheral +3.3 V rail is supplied only by Pico header 36 and powers U7/U10. Do not connect a plug-in module's 3.3 V output to it. Fit seven local 100 nF capacitors, three 22 uF board capacitors, and one 100 uF entry capacitor. Observe electrolytic polarity; the 1N5819 band faces VSYS.

All installed 5 V ICs must be powered whenever the 5 V rail is on. Pulls do not isolate installed unpowered devices. Follow Phase 0.

docs.title: 3.2 KiCad Electrical Schematic
docs.text:
The native schematic and net manifest are generated by build-kicad-schematic.py. Current validation: zero ERC violations, 71 real nets, 284 pin endpoints. This establishes connectivity, not bench timing or supply-transient safety.

The existing PCB, session, Gerbers, drills, and PCB assembly outputs are unchanged and belong to the previous circuit. Do not manufacture them for the assisted-loader revision. Do not run the full PCB regeneration pipeline until a separate PCB migration is authorized.

docs.title: 0. Project Inventory
docs.text:
This is the eight-active-package assisted-loader design, excluding the power diode. No PLD, PLD programmer, address expander, or reset transistor is needed. Match the complete part number and PDIP package before ordering.

Tick an item when you have the full listed quantity available, including the specified socket or headers where applicable. These are inventory checks, not installation or electrical-test results. Progress is saved in this browser on this device, separately from the implementation-phase checklists.

Clear checklist

docs.title: Permanent breadboard resistors
docs.text:
Use 39 individual (discrete) 10 kOhm resistors. No resistor-network packages are fitted on the breadboard. Each resistor connects one signal to its specified supply rail or GND; signal wires must not be joined together. A resistor to a supply is a pull-up, and a resistor to GND is a pull-down. These establish defaults when no active output drives a signal.

The group checks below divide the same 39 resistors listed above; they are not additional parts. Tick each group when its quantity is set aside.

docs.title: Purpose and instrument limits
docs.text:
The DSLogic Plus proves simultaneous digital state, event ordering, bus values, and control sequencing. It complements the RIGOL DHO814: the logic analyzer answers what happened and in what order, while the oscilloscope proves voltage margin, rise/fall time, ringing, overshoot, and close analogue timing. Never use a logic-analyzer HIGH or LOW display as proof that a receiving device's datasheet voltage limits were met.

A displayed bus value is only as correct as the channel mapping: label the channels before capture and put bit 0 at the least-significant position. The analyzer samples rather than recording every instant; at 100 MHz, samples are 10 ns apart, so a shorter pulse may be missed. A clean-looking digital trace is not proof that the analog waveform has no glitch.

The official DSLogic Plus data sheet specifies:

Property DSLogic Plus limit Digital channels 16, CH0-CH15 Buffer Mode sample rate 400 MHz / 4 channels, 200 MHz / 8 channels, 100 MHz / 16 channels Stream Mode sample rate 100 MHz / 3 channels, 50 MHz / 6 channels, 25 MHz / 12 channels, 20 MHz / 16 channels Hardware memory 256 Mbits Buffer depth without RLE 256 Mbits divided by enabled channel count Maximum stream depth 16G samples Input threshold 0-5 V, adjustable in 0.1 V steps Input impedance 250 kOhm in parallel with approximately 13 pF Protected CH0-CH15 range -30 V to +30 V with the supplied fly wires 100 MHz timing accuracy Within one sample interval, approximately +/-10 ns per captured edge

All 16 channels are required for a complete address-bus capture, so this project uses 16-channel, 100 MHz Buffer Mode for qualification. At the experimental 8 MHz clock limit this gives 12.5 samples per clock period, satisfying DSView's recommendation to use at least 10 times the measured signal frequency when phase accuracy matters. It cannot resolve analogue behavior or prove a timing margin smaller than its sample uncertainty; use the DHO814 capture plan for those cases.

The 16-channel Stream Mode limit is 20 MHz, only 2.5 samples per 8 MHz clock. Use it for long-duration state/fault searches at low clock rates, not as timing qualification evidence at the final operating frequency.

docs.title: Safety and connection preparation
docs.text:
1. Install the current DSView release from the DreamSourceLab download page. Connect DSLogic Plus directly to a reliable USB port. Open DSView and require the hardware indicator to turn green and the device selector to identify DSLogic Plus before attaching it to the circuit.
  2. The probe grounds are connected through USB to the host computer ground. Connect them only to the SBC's common GND. Never attach a ground lead to +3.3 V, +5 V, a signal, or a floating/hot DUT. If the host is mains-grounded, DSLogic ground is earth-referenced.
  3. Power off the SBC before attaching or moving clips. Connect ground leads first, then signal leads. Remove signal leads first when disconnecting.
  4. Use the supplied shielded fly wires. Each active channel has an independent ground return; connect those returns to nearby common-GND points. Although the Z80 clock is at most 8 MHz, its edges are fast, so use the guide's high-frequency connection method rather than one long shared ground lead.
  5. Probe the physical destination pin listed below, not a distant jumper end. Sixteen inputs add meaningful capacitive loading to a solderless breadboard. Recheck operation at 1 MHz after connecting each group, and do not stack a scope probe on the same node unless that combined loaded condition is the test being qualified.
  6. Do not connect CK, TI, or TO for the standard project captures. CK and TI are limited to the 0-3.3 V domain; attaching either to a 5 V Z80 signal violates the hardware data sheet. CH0-CH15 provide every trigger used here.

docs.title: Baseline DSView configuration
docs.text:
1. Press O or open Options. Select Logic Analyzer and Buffer Mode, with Upload captured data as the stop option.
  2. Select Use 16 Channels (Max 100 MHz), enable CH0-CH15, set Sample Rate = 100 MHz, and begin with Sample Duration = 100 ms. The official maximum at 100 MHz with 16 channels is approximately 167.77 ms.
  3. Set Filter Targets = None. The 1 Sample Clock filter suppresses pulses shorter than one sample interval and must not be used as pass evidence.
  4. Disable RLE Compress for baseline qualification so capture depth is fixed and reproducible. A separately labelled RLE capture may be used to search for sparse events, but it does not replace the baseline capture.
  5. Set the single device threshold for the selected group: 3.5 V for Group A, 2.2 V for Group B, or 1.6 V for mixed 3.3 V/TTL Groups C and D. These thresholds make transitions visible at useful digital decision levels; the DHO814 still proves device-specific $V_{IH}$/$V_{IL}$ margins.
  6. Select Single Capture and Normal Capture. Do not use Instant Capture as pass evidence because it ignores trigger settings. Repetitive Capture is useful only as additional evidence for repeatable events.
  7. Press T to open Trigger. Use Simple Trigger unless a scenario below requests a bus pattern. Clear every stale channel condition first: multiple Simple Trigger conditions are ANDed at the same sample point.
  8. Start with the trigger position at 30% to retain the cause and more post-trigger response. Use 50% when equal pre/post context is useful. Stream Mode fixes the trigger close to the start and is not used for these gates.
  9. Rename every channel to the signal shown in its group before capture. Use cursors and edge snap to measure ordering; record the sample count between relevant edges as well as the displayed time.
  10. Save the complete .dsl capture and DSView session, export a VCD or raw CSV, and save a PNG screenshot. Include phase, clock rate, stimulus, group, threshold, sample rate, duration, filter, RLE state, and trigger in the name.

docs.title: Trigger and expected outcomes
docs.text:
Purpose Group and trigger Expected result Address integrity Group A. Set all 16 Simple Trigger levels to match 0000, FFFF, 5555, or AAAA; all conditions are ANDed. Repeat for each fixed pattern and trigger on 0000 for walking/CPU-read sequences. Every captured word equals the commanded address, each walking pattern changes only the intended bit, and no address transition occurs during the active sampling interval of a memory cycle. Repeat at every qualified clock rate. Opcode fetch Group B, CH15 M1# falling. M1#, MREQ#, RD#, CE#, and OE# assert in the expected active-LOW sequence; WE# remains HIGH and D0-D7 contain the fetched opcode before the Z80 sampling edge. SRAM read Group B, CH10 RD# falling with CH9 MREQ# LOW. CE# and OE# assert once, WE# remains HIGH, and all eight data bits settle to the expected byte before the sampling edge. No extra control transition is permitted. SRAM write Group B, CH11 WR# falling with CH9 MREQ# LOW. D0-D7 contain the expected byte before WE# falls and remain stable through its LOW pulse; CE# and WE# assert once and OE# remains HIGH. DSLogic screens pulse presence and ordering only; the DHO814 must prove the exact 45 ns minimum WE# LOW width. Reset and restart Group D, CH0 RESET# rising, trigger position 30%. RESET# was LOW for six complete clocks. Injection starts with inhibit HIGH after the two exit clocks. Normal restart has both data paths isolated and inhibit LOW; CPU controls alone operate SRAM. Verify real reset-exit phase before accepting the cycle model. Flash quiescence Group D, CH2 BUSACK# falling for acquisition; repeat rising for release. BUSREQ# falls before BUSACK#. CPU address/control outputs float; pulls make SRAM controls inactive. Pico does not drive memory. Trap is armed before BUSREQ# release. Injected loading Group D, CH12 inhibit and CH4 RD# edges. SRAM OE# stays HIGH during injected instructions. It falls only for a deliberate SRAM read, with Pico output isolated. SRAM WE# follows CPU writes, never a Pico-generated write pulse. Trapped IN Group C with RD# on CH10; trigger CH9 IORQ# falling. WAIT# falls before sampling. Only AHCT245 OE# falls; the Pico supplies the reply byte. GP9 releases WAIT after preload. Slow clocks complete the cycle; both OEs are HIGH and GP9 LOW before PWM resumes. Trapped OUT Group C with WR# on CH10; trigger CH9 IORQ# falling. WAIT# falls first. Only LVC245 OE# falls; the Pico samples the CPU byte. GP9 releases WAIT. Stepped completion isolates/rearms before PWM. The two OE# signals are never LOW together.

For the final frequency claim, save Group A, B, C-IN, C-OUT, and D captures at each tested rate. The separate groups must use the same firmware build, clock rate, and deterministic stimulus. A 16-channel DSLogic Plus cannot establish simultaneous whole-address, whole-data, and control ordering in one acquisition; do not imply otherwise in qualification records.

docs.text:

  • DSView User Guide
