docs.title: Appendix A: Terms and Abbreviations
docs.text:
This glossary explains the recurring terminology used in this document. Signal names ending in # are active LOW: for example, RESET# is asserted (active) at 0 V and deasserted (inactive) at a valid HIGH voltage. An overbar or _N suffix in a datasheet or source file commonly means the same thing.

For example, firmware gpio_put(PIN_RESET_N, 0) asserts reset and keeps the CPU from running. Writing 1 releases reset. HIGH means a valid voltage in that signal's domain, not always 5 V: the Z80 RESET# node is driven directly by a 3.3 V Pico output. Neither a HIGH reading nor a Hi-Z output means it is safe to connect that node to an arbitrary supply.

docs.title: System and Processor Terms
docs.text: Term Meaning Purpose in this project SBC Single-board computer The complete Z80 computer built across the three breadboards. Z80 Zilog 8-bit microprocessor family Executes the monitor, test programs, and CP/M after the Pico loads SRAM. CPU Central processing unit The Z84C0020PEC Z80 that executes program instructions. Pico / Pico 2 W Raspberry Pi Pico 2 W microcontroller board Supervises startup, loads SRAM, traps I/O, provides virtual disks, and hosts the Wi-Fi terminal. Supervisor Controller responsible for safe startup and system management Pico firmware owns reset, clock, assisted loading, trapped I/O, and faults. Bus Shared group of electrical signals Carries addresses, data, or controls between Z80, SRAM, and buffered Pico interface. Address bus / A0-A15 Sixteen wires selecting a memory location or I/O port Addresses 65,536 byte locations; A0 is the least-significant bit and A15 the most-significant bit. Data bus / D0-D7 Eight bidirectional wires carrying one byte Transfers instruction, memory, and I/O data between devices. Control bus Timing and ownership signals such as MREQ#, RD#, and BUSACK# Identifies the type and phase of each Z80 transaction. I/O Input/output Communication with peripherals rather than ordinary memory. This design implements most peripherals in Pico firmware. Port An I/O address selected by a Z80 IN or OUT instruction Selects terminal, disk, status, or other virtual-device registers. Trap Firmware interception of a Z80 I/O cycle Stops the static Z80 clock so the Pico can inspect or complete the cycle. Assisted loader CPU-executed RAM loading Pico injects LD HL,nn, LD (HL),n and LD A,(HL); Z80 alone drives addresses and writes. DMA buffer CP/M software transfer address BIOS SETDMA selects a RAM buffer; it does not give Pico hardware bus-master capability. ROMless Having no physical Z80 ROM Injected instructions populate SRAM, followed by a reset to execute the verified image. Static CPU CPU whose clock may be stopped without losing internal state Allows the Pico to freeze the Z80 safely during a trapped I/O cycle. Clock / CLK Repeating timing signal Advances the Z80 state machine; generated by the Pico and translated by the AHCT244. Machine cycle Group of clock periods used for one bus operation Defines when addresses, controls, and data must become valid. Wait state Extra clock period inserted into a bus cycle HCT32 WAIT holds I/O until GP9 releases it. Ordinary SRAM cycles have no added memory waits.

docs.title: Memory, Storage, and Software Terms
docs.text: Term Meaning Purpose in this project RAM Random-access memory Read/write working memory; contents are normally lost when power is removed. SRAM Static random-access memory The AS6C1008 provides the Z80's 64 KiB address space and needs no refresh clock. Flash Nonvolatile electrically erasable storage Pico onboard flash holds firmware, the Z80 boot package, CP/M disks, and the write journal. XIP Execute in place Pico address mapping that permits flash contents to be read like ordinary memory. CP/M Control Program for Microcomputers The disk operating system run by the Z80. BIOS Basic Input/Output System CP/M's board-specific layer for console and disk access. It is unrelated to a modern PC BIOS. BDOS Basic Disk Operating System CP/M service layer implementing files, console functions, and other operating-system calls. CCP Console Command Processor CP/M command interpreter that reads and runs commands. DPB Disk Parameter Block CP/M table describing logical disk geometry and allocation rules. LBA Logical block address Linear number identifying one 128-byte virtual-disk record. Sector / record Fixed-size disk transfer unit CP/M exchanges one 128-byte record; flash updates preserve its containing 4 KiB erase sector. Journal Temporary recovery record written before changing disk data Allows an interrupted flash write to recover the complete old or new block after reboot. Manifest Header describing an image and its integrity data Gives boot-image length, version, and CRC values before SRAM loading. CRC / CRC32 Cyclic redundancy check, using a 32-bit result here Detects corruption in boot images, journal entries, and generated artifacts. SHA-256 256-bit cryptographic hash Records reproducible host-artifact identities; it is not calculated by the Z80. Firmware Software executed by a microcontroller The phase-based Pico applications under src/. Boot loader Code that prepares and starts another program Validates the flash package, copies the Z80 image to SRAM, then releases reset. UF2 USB Flashing Format Drag-and-drop or picotool firmware image format supported by Pico boot ROM. BOOTSEL Pico USB boot-selection mode Allows firmware or complete flash images to be loaded while the application is not running.

docs.title: Digital Electronics Terms
docs.text: Term Meaning Purpose in this project GPIO General-purpose input/output Individually programmable Pico pins used for clocks, controls, buses, and status. PWM Pulse-width modulation hardware Pico peripheral used to generate an accurate, variable-frequency Z80 clock. SIO Single-cycle I/O block in the RP2350 Direct Pico GPIO hardware used for static levels and manual clock stepping; not Z80 serial I/O. IRQ Interrupt request Hardware event that diverts Pico execution to the I/O trap handler. ISR / handler Interrupt service routine Time-critical Pico function that freezes and services a trapped Z80 cycle. OR gate Output HIGH when either input is HIGH HCT32 gates SRAM reads, WAIT release, and Pico-to-bus output. Static hazard / glitch Unwanted short output pulse caused by unequal logic delays Must be checked at SRAM and CPU pins; a clean logical netlist does not prove analogue timing. Buffer Logic device that strengthens, isolates, or translates a signal AHCT244 drives 5 V clock/control signals; LVC244 protects all eight monitored inputs. Transceiver Bidirectional or direction-controlled bus buffer AHCT245 and LVC245 form separate Pico-to-bus and bus-to-Pico data paths. Tri-state / high-impedance / Hi-Z Output state that electrically disconnects its driver Permits several devices to share a bus as long as only the intended owner drives it. Bus contention Two outputs driving different levels on one wire Can damage parts. Firmware must disable both data paths before switching; RD gating is not an all-state interlock. Level shifting / translation Converting signals between voltage domains Connects Pico 3.3 V logic to 5 V Z80, SRAM, and HCT32 without raw 5 V input paths. 5 V tolerant Input may safely receive a specified 5 V-domain signal Required for every path from installed 5 V logic into a 3.3 V-powered device. Ioff Partial-power-down input/output protection Prevents LVC devices from being back-powered through their pins while their supply is off. Pull-up / pull-down Resistor weakly biasing a signal HIGH / LOW Establishes a safe default when no active device drives the signal. Decoupling / bypass capacitor Small capacitor beside an IC supply pair Supplies brief switching current locally and suppresses rail noise. Bulk capacitor Larger capacitor on a board or supply entry Reduces slower supply dips; it does not replace local decoupling. Power domain / rail Group of devices sharing a supply voltage The design has regulated 5 V logic and Pico-derived 3.3 V logic domains with common ground. GND Common electrical reference, nominally 0 V Return path and voltage reference shared by all boards and instruments. VCC / VDD Positive IC supply voltage Usually 5 V for Z80-side logic and 3.3 V for Pico-side LVC devices in this design. VSYS / VBUS / 3V3 Pico system-input, USB 5 V, and regulated 3.3 V rails Must be connected exactly as specified to avoid back-powering USB or the Pico regulator. Schottky diode Low-forward-voltage diode The 1N5819 safely ORs external 5 V into Pico VSYS.

docs.title: Signal Names and Bus Notation
docs.text:
The descriptions below state the signal's purpose when it is asserted. Because most Z80 controls are active LOW, an inactive signal normally sits HIGH.

Signal or notation Meaning Purpose in this project CLK Clock Advances the Z80. The Pico generates it and the AHCT244 translates it to a compliant 5 V clock level. RESET# Reset LOW initializes the Z80. It does not select any Pico memory controls. BUSREQ# Bus request LOW asks the Z80 to float its buses for runtime flash quiescence, not Pico memory access. BUSACK# Bus acknowledge LOW confirms the CPU bus grant before a flash erase/program operation. MREQ# Memory request Z80 drives it LOW during a memory transaction; becomes the CPU-owned source for SRAM CE#. IORQ# Input/output request Z80 drives it LOW during an I/O transaction; its falling edge starts the Pico clock-stop trap. RD# Read Z80 drives it LOW when the selected memory or I/O device must place data onto D0-D7. WR# Write Z80 drives it LOW when the selected memory or I/O device must accept data from D0-D7. M1# Machine-cycle-one Z80 drives it LOW during an opcode fetch and interrupt acknowledgement; used here as a Phase 6 reset/fetch probe point. RFSH# Dynamic-memory refresh Z80 output for refreshing DRAM after an opcode fetch; this SRAM design does not use it. HALT# Halt state Z80 drives it LOW after executing HALT; not connected to the Pico in this design. WAIT# Wait request HCT32 pin 6 computes IORQ# OR IO_RELEASE. GP9 remains HIGH until the I/O controls release. No WAIT pull-up is fitted. INT# Maskable interrupt request An external device could pull it LOW to request a normal Z80 interrupt; unused and pulled HIGH here. NMI# Non-maskable interrupt request A falling edge requests the Z80's highest-priority interrupt; unused and pulled HIGH here. CE# Chip enable LOW selects SRAM; buffered CPU MREQ# is the only source. CE2 Second chip-enable input Active-HIGH SRAM enable tied permanently to 5 V; CE# remains the switched enable. OE# Output enable LOW allows a memory, buffer, or transceiver to drive its output pins. WE# Write enable LOW commands SRAM to store the current data-bus value. DIR Fixed transceiver direction U9 DIR is +5 V; U10 DIR is GND. No firmware direction pin exists. BOOT_READ_DISABLE SRAM-read inhibit GP5, buffered to HCT32, keeps SRAM OE# HIGH during injection. IO_RELEASE Independent WAIT release GP9 allows the stalled I/O cycle to finish after data is ready. PICO_DATA_UP_OE# Output-enable request GP6 OR raw RD# produces actual U9 DATA_UP_OE#. DATA_UP_OE# Actual Pico-to-bus enable HCT32 pin 8 drives AHCT245 pin 19. LOW drives a byte only with RD# LOW. DATA_DOWN_OE# Bus-to-Pico enable GP7 directly drives LVC245 pin 19. LOW receives CPU/SRAM data. PICO_* / Z80_* Source-name prefix Distinguishes Pico-generated controls from Z80-generated controls in equations and net names. A0-A15 Address bits 0 through 15 Shared 16-bit address bus; A0 is least significant and A15 most significant. A16 SRAM address bit 16 Tied LOW so only the lower 64 KiB of the 128 KiB SRAM is used. D0-D7 Data bits 0 through 7 Shared 8-bit bidirectional data bus; D0 is least significant. IN / OUT Z80 input / output instructions Read a byte from, or write a byte to, an I/O port serviced by the Pico trap. #, _N, or overbar Active-LOW notation Indicates that LOW means asserted. For example, PIN_RD_N in source code represents hardware RD#. X in a truth table Don't-care value Either LOW or HIGH is allowed because that input cannot alter the stated result.

docs.title: Component Names and Pin Labels
docs.text: Name or fragment Meaning Purpose in this project Z84C0020PEC Zilog CMOS Z80, 20 MHz grade, plastic DIP commercial part The exact CPU specified for the build; 20 MHz is a part rating, not the qualified system speed. AS6C1008-55PCN Alliance Memory 128 KiB x 8 SRAM, 55 ns, plastic DIP Provides the Z80's lower 64 KiB memory space. SN74HCT32N / HCT32 Quad OR gate with TTL-compatible inputs Fixed boot-inhibit, WAIT-release, and data-strobe gating; HC32 is not a substitute. SN74AHCT244N / AHCT244 8-channel non-inverting 5 V buffer with TTL inputs Translates clock, bus request, boot inhibit, and Z80 SRAM controls. SN74AHCT245N / AHCT245 8-bit 5 V bus transceiver with TTL inputs Implements the fixed Pico-to-5 V data path. SN74LVC245AN / LVC245 8-bit low-voltage bus transceiver with 5 V-tolerant inputs Implements the fixed 5 V-to-Pico data path. SN74LVC244AN / LVC244 8-channel low-voltage buffer with 5 V-tolerant inputs Buffers BUSACK/IORQ/RD/WR and A0/A1/A2/A4 into the Pico domain. 1N5819 Schottky rectifier diode ORs external 5 V into Pico VSYS without feeding the USB VBUS node. A1-A8 / B1-B8 The two eight-bit ports of a 245 transceiver A faces the Pico and B faces the 5 V bus in this design. 1A1, 1Y1, etc. Input and output labels on a 244/541 buffer bank A is a buffer input and Y is its corresponding output; the leading digit selects a bank where present. OE1# / OE2# Output-enable inputs for buffer bank 1 / 2 Tied LOW on the always-readable LVC244 and AHCT244 buffers. A 245 transceiver instead has one OE# for all eight bits. GP0, GP1, etc. Pico general-purpose pin number RP2350 GPIO index used by firmware; it is not the Pico header's physical pin number. pin 1, notch, dot Package orientation references Identify how to insert a device without rotation or mirroring. N, AN, PCN, PEC, PU, SP suffixes Manufacturer package/grade codes Distinguish exact orderable parts; consult that manufacturer's datasheet rather than assuming suffixes are interchangeable.

docs.title: Pico Pad and Power Terms
docs.text: Term Meaning Purpose in this project RP2350 Microcontroller chip used by Pico 2 W Executes the supervisor firmware and provides GPIO, PWM, flash access, and two CPU cores. GP0-GP29 RP2350 GPIO numbers exposed or used by Pico 2 W Firmware-level pin names; map them to physical header pins with the Pico header map. Pad Physical input/output cell on the RP2350 die Determines electrical properties such as 5 V tolerance and ADC capability. FT pad Five-volt-tolerant digital pad GP0-GP25 pad type; tolerance still depends on RP2350 power conditions. ADC pad Analog-to-digital-converter-capable pad GP26-GP29 pad type; not 5 V tolerant, so GP27/GP28 monitors require the LVC244. ADC Analog-to-digital converter Converts voltage to a number; not used for Z80 monitoring despite GP26-GP29 being ADC-capable. IOVDD RP2350 input/output supply Must be present at 3.3 V for the FT-pad 5.5 V absolute-maximum condition to apply. AGND Pico analog ground pin Bonded to common ground because this project does not use a separate analog subsystem. ADC_VREF Pico ADC reference-voltage pin Left open because the project does not use Pico ADC measurements. 3V3 / 3V3(OUT) Pico regulated 3.3 V output Powers LVC244/LVC245 and 3.3 V pull-ups. 3V3_EN Pico 3.3 V regulator enable Left open; pulling it LOW would disable the Pico's 3.3 V rail. RUN Pico reset input Left open; pulling it LOW resets the RP2350. VBUS USB connector's nominal 5 V node Must not be tied to the external 5 V rail. VSYS Pico system power input Receives external 5 V only through the 1N5819 and USB power through Pico's onboard diode. Core 0 / Core 1 The two RP2350 processor cores Core 0 owns timing and buses; core 1 owns networking and runtime flash writes. FIFO First-in, first-out queue Ordered communication buffer; the multicore FIFO is reserved by Pico flash lockout support.

docs.title: Software, Network, File, and Test Abbreviations
docs.text: Term Meaning Purpose in this project SDK Software development kit Pico headers, libraries, tools, and build support used by the firmware. API Application programming interface Defined functions through which code or tools access a subsystem. CLI Command-line interface Text-based invocation of tools such as CMake, picotool, and test scripts. CI Continuous integration Automated build/test environment that can reject boundary or artifact failures. USB Universal Serial Bus Programs the Pico, carries diagnostics, and connects test instruments to the Mac. UART Universal asynchronous receiver/transmitter Common serial protocol supported by decoders; the Z80 terminal itself is virtual, not a UART chip. I2C / I²C Inter-Integrated Circuit Two-wire serial protocol supported by instruments but not used for the CPU/SRAM interface. TCP/IP Transmission Control Protocol / Internet Protocol Networking foundation used by HTTP and WebSocket traffic. HTTP Hypertext Transfer Protocol Serves the browser terminal page from Pico port 8088. HTML Hypertext Markup Language Source format of the embedded browser terminal interface. JSON JavaScript Object Notation Structured text format used for generated manifests. CSV Comma-separated values Plain-text tabular export format for captures, measurements, and generated data. SVG Scalable Vector Graphics Vector image format used for diagrams and schematic exports. PDF Portable Document Format Generated printable edition of this specification and schematic. FFT Fast Fourier transform Converts sampled time-domain data into a frequency spectrum. DVM Digital voltmeter Instrument function that reports numeric voltage measurements. RLE Run-length encoding Compression that stores repeated identical digital samples efficiently. IEEE CRC32 Standard 32-bit CRC convention Exact CRC algorithm used by boot and journal formats. XIP_BASE Base address of Pico's memory-mapped external flash Added to a flash offset to obtain a readable pointer. PICO_OK Pico SDK success result Required return from flash_safe_execute() before a flash operation is accepted. watchdog Hardware recovery timer Reboots into journal recovery if runtime flash coordination cannot continue safely. atomic Operation observed as indivisible between cores Protects shared status words without a lock needed by the trap. nonblocking Returns immediately rather than waiting Required for trap hooks and foreground services that must not stall another critical task. CRC, hash, verify Different integrity checks CRC detects transfer/storage corruption, SHA-256 identifies host artifacts, and verify compares programmed/read-back contents.

docs.title: Units, Numeric Notation, and Data Sizes
docs.text: Notation Meaning How to read it here 0x prefix Hexadecimal (base-16) number 0xFF is decimal 255; convenient for bytes, addresses, masks, and register values. bit One binary digit Has value 0 or 1. Eight bits form one byte. byte Eight bits One Z80 data-bus transfer and one addressable SRAM location. K, M, G in rates Decimal kilo, mega, giga Multipliers of 1,000; for example, 1 MHz is 1,000,000 cycles per second. KiB / MiB Kibibyte / mebibyte Binary sizes of 1,024 bytes / 1,048,576 bytes. KB / MB Kilobyte / megabyte Sometimes used informally in prose or vendor material; exact project image sizes are stated in bytes or KiB. Hz, kHz, MHz Hertz, kilohertz, megahertz Cycles per second; used for clock, signal, and bandwidth values. S/s, MS/s, GSa/s Samples per second, mega-samples/s, giga-samples/s Logic-analyzer or oscilloscope sampling rate, not signal frequency. s, ms, us, ns Second, millisecond, microsecond, nanosecond Time units: each step is one thousand times smaller than the previous. Source identifiers use us for microseconds. V, mV Volt, millivolt Electrical potential; 1 V equals 1,000 mV. A, mA Ampere, milliampere Electrical current; 1 A equals 1,000 mA. Ohm, kOhm Ohm, kilo-ohm Resistance; 10 kOhm means 10,000 ohms. pF, nF, uF Picofarad, nanofarad, microfarad Capacitance units; adjacent steps differ by 1,000. uF is ASCII notation for µF. Mpts, samples Million points / recorded measurements Capture-memory depth; available duration depends on sample rate and active channels. x or × Multiplication or count 128K x 8 means 128K locations each eight bits wide; 8x10 kOhm means eight resistors. 1x / 10x Probe attenuation Probe delivers full voltage / one tenth voltage to the scope; software must use the matching setting.

docs.title: Logic Families, Levels, and Timing
docs.text: Term Meaning Purpose in this project TTL Transistor-transistor logic levels A TTL-compatible input accepts a lower HIGH voltage than a 5 V CMOS input. CMOS Complementary metal-oxide-semiconductor logic Technology used by the static Z80, SRAM, Pico, and most interface devices. HCT High-speed CMOS with TTL-compatible inputs HCT32 implements SRAM-read inhibit, WAIT release, and upward data-enable gating. HC32 is not a substitute. AHCT Advanced high-speed CMOS with TTL-compatible inputs AHCT244 translates clock, bus request, boot inhibit, and SRAM controls; AHCT245 drives the 5 V data bus from Pico 3.3 V outputs. LVC Low-voltage CMOS logic family LVC244/LVC245 run at 3.3 V while accepting protected 5 V inputs. HIGH / LOW The two digital logic states Voltage ranges, not exact voltages; valid limits are defined by each datasheet. Assert / deassert Make a control active / inactive Independent of voltage wording; asserting RESET# means driving it LOW. $V_{IH}$ / $V_{IL}$ Minimum input-HIGH / maximum input-LOW voltage Determines whether a receiving input is guaranteed to recognize a signal. $V_{OH}$ / $V_{OL}$ Guaranteed output-HIGH / output-LOW voltage Determines whether a driver meets the receiving device's input thresholds under load. Propagation delay Time from input transition to output response AHCT244/HCT32 delays and SRAM access constrain clock rate and sampling margin. Setup time Time data must be stable before a sampling clock edge SRAM read data must arrive early enough for the Z80 to sample it correctly. Hold time Time data must remain stable after a sampling edge Drivers must not release or change the bus too soon. Rise / fall time Time for a signal edge to change between LOW and HIGH Fast edges, rather than only clock frequency, cause breadboard ringing and crosstalk. Duty cycle Percentage of a period that a signal is HIGH The Z80 clock is targeted at 50%, with a stated acceptance range. Ringing / overshoot Oscillation or voltage excursion following an edge Can cross logic thresholds or exceed ratings; checked with short-ground scope probing. Crosstalk Unwanted coupling from one signal into another Reduced by short grouped wiring and nearby ground returns. Timing margin Remaining safe time or voltage beyond a required limit Measured during qualification rather than inferred from part speed ratings alone.

docs.title: Package, Construction, and Schematic Terms
docs.text: Term Meaning Purpose in this project IC Integrated circuit A packaged electronic device such as the Z80, SRAM, or logic buffer. DIP / PDIP Dual in-line package / plastic dual in-line package Through-hole IC package with two parallel pin rows, suitable for sockets and breadboards. Discrete resistor One resistor in its own component body The breadboard uses 39 individual 10 kOhm resistors, not packaged resistor networks. Pin 1 / notch / dot Package orientation marks Prevent an IC from being inserted rotated or mirrored. Breadboard ravine Insulating center gap of a solderless breadboard Separates the two IC pin rows so opposite pins are not shorted together. Net All electrically connected points sharing one signal name Fundamental connection represented and checked in the KiCad schematic. Junction Explicit connection where wires meet Distinguishes an intended shared node from crossing but unconnected wires. ERC Electrical rules check KiCad check for incompatible, missing, or improperly driven schematic connections. Netlist Machine-readable list of components, pins, and nets Independently compared with the generated manifest to validate schematic connectivity. BOM Bill of materials List and quantity of components needed to build the system.

docs.title: Measurement and Build Terms
docs.text: Term Meaning Purpose in this project Oscilloscope / scope Instrument displaying voltage versus time Measures analog levels, edge shape, pulse width, ringing, and timing between two signals. Logic analyzer Instrument recording many digital HIGH/LOW signals The 16-channel DSLogic Plus correlates bus values and control ordering in repeated capture groups. Buffer Mode DSLogic mode that captures into onboard memory before uploading Provides 100 MHz sampling with all 16 channels for project qualification captures. Stream Mode DSLogic mode that transfers samples continuously over USB Extends duration, but all 16 channels are limited to 20 MHz and are unsuitable for final 8 MHz timing qualification. Input threshold Voltage at which a logic analyzer changes its displayed digital state DSLogic Plus provides a global adjustable threshold; it does not replace device-specific analogue $V_{IH}$/$V_{IL}$ checks. RLE Run-length encoding Optional DSLogic compression for sparse Buffer Mode activity; disabled for fixed-depth baseline evidence. MSO Mixed-signal oscilloscope Instrument combining analog scope channels with synchronized digital inputs; the DHO814 has four analog channels but no integrated digital bus inputs. Probe Instrument lead designed to minimize loading A compensated 10x scope probe is used for analog measurements; logic probes capture digital states. 1x / 10x probe Probe attenuation ratio 10x mode usually loads fast logic less and provides better bandwidth than 1x mode. Ground spring Very short probe-ground attachment Prevents the probe's own ground-loop inductance from creating apparent ringing. Bandwidth Highest sine-wave frequency passed within a stated attenuation The DHO814's 100 MHz front end has an approximate 3.5 ns calculated rise-time limit; with the supplied 150 MHz probe, the combined measurement-system limit is about 4.2 ns. Sample rate Number of measurements recorded per second Determines time resolution; it is distinct from analog bandwidth. Real-time sampling Samples used for one displayed acquisition are collected from the same trigger event The DHO814 uses real-time sampling, so Single mode can preserve a one-off transition for analysis. Memory depth Number of samples retained in one acquisition The DHO814 provides up to 25 Mpts, allowing substantial pre-trigger and post-trigger context while retaining a useful sample rate. AWG Arbitrary waveform generator Produces programmable test waveforms; available in many USB scopes but not required for Z80 operation. SCPI Standard Commands for Programmable Instruments Text-command interface for automating compatible bench instruments. KiCad Electronic schematic and PCB design application Holds the native electrical schematic and runs ERC. CMake / Ninja Build-system generator / build executor Configure and compile the Pico firmware and generated CP/M artifacts. Toolchain Compiler, assembler, linker, libraries, and utilities Converts source code into executable Pico and Z80 images. Bare metal Software running without a hosted desktop operating system The Pico firmware links its own embedded runtime rather than macOS libraries. lwIP Lightweight IP networking stack Supplies TCP/IP networking used by the Pico WebSocket terminal. WebSocket Persistent bidirectional browser/server connection Carries terminal bytes between the browser and Pico with low overhead.

docs.title: 7. Reference Firmware Implementations
docs.text:
The maintained, buildable firmware is the canonical implementation: browse the source tree or use the complete source index. The corresponding implementation phase pages embed complete source files in collapsible sections alongside explanations of the safety invariants and integration order: variable-frequency clock generation, bus acquisition, synchronous I/O trapping, flash image loading, and terminal integration. The code is included directly from the checkout at documentation build time. Build from the repository rather than copying displayed files into a separate project.

For one complete fresh-checkout workflow covering native C tests, hardware test replacements, Z80 emulation, real SDK cross-builds and their limitations, see Building and Testing Pico C Firmware.

docs.title: Breadboard-first, shared Pico firmware
docs.text:
The phase-based Pico applications remain focused on the breadboard construction and bring-up plan. The existing PCB is for the superseded circuit and is not compatible with this firmware. Its migration is deferred; do not manufacture it or use the new firmware on that layout without separately updating wiring.

Keep the shared defaults conservative. Phase 10 explicitly inherits the tested Phase 9 automatic loader's 20 MHz operating setting, not the previous Phase 10 1 MHz default. This does not qualify combined Wi-Fi/storage operation or the deferred PCB. Operating-frequency qualification remains specific to each physical build.

All phase firmware targets configure clk_sys to 144 MHz at SDK startup. The 12 MHz crystal feeds PLL_SYS with reference divider 1, a 1440 MHz VCO, and post-dividers 5 and 2. This stays within the RP2350's rated limits and lets integer PWM generate a nominally exact 8 MHz Z80 clock (144 MHz / 18) with 50% duty cycle. USB keeps its separate 48 MHz PLL; peripheral/PIO timing uses the configured system clock. This does not change the 1 MHz Z80 startup default or qualify 8 MHz hardware operation. See the frequency qualification plan.

Phases 9 and 10 are explicit exceptions: after safe startup and before initializing USB it selects a 120 MHz supervisor clock, then uses 20 MHz PWM only after complete SRAM loading/verification. The diagnostic variant starts on command; the automatic loader starts on Pico reset without waiting for USB. Their clock/CPU/trap chain is compiled separately with the existing 20 MHz opt-in; other phases retain their own limits/defaults. The 20 MHz frequency is scope-measured on the project prototype; this does not qualify integrated CP/M, disk I/O or signal margins.

Shared firmware does not make every early-phase diagnostic safe on a fully populated PCB. Respect each phase's required device population and test preconditions, especially walking-output tests intended for empty destination sockets.

docs.title: Choose the image for your current phase
docs.text:
There are two processors and two kinds of software: Pico firmware runs the supervisor and diagnostics; Z80 programs run from SRAM after the Pico loads them by feeding instructions to the Z80. No PLD or external programmer is required; the HCT32 implements fixed combinational logic.

During construction, load only the Pico firmware matching the phase of hardware you have installed. Phase 10 and the complete flash image assume the whole circuit is ready; they are not substitutes for Phase 1 diagnostics. The phase pages link their maintained applications, and the source index lists the corresponding source directories.

Phase numbers match the NN values in source directory names, not the documentation's section numbers (for example, section 8.2 is Phase 1). Directory names describe the firmware diagnostic, so they need not repeat the hardware phase title. src/stage00_power/ contains only a checklist: Phase 0 has no Pico firmware or build target.

Phase Source directory CMake target 1 src/stage01_supervisor/ z80_stage01_supervisor 2 src/stage02_buffers_clock/ z80_stage02_buffers_clock 3 src/stage03_mcp23s17/ z80_stage03_control_inputs 4 src/stage04_address_bus/ z80_stage04_address_bus 5 src/stage05_data_bus/ z80_stage05_data_bus 6 src/stage06_sram_dma/ z80_stage06_sram_loader 6 bus grants src/stage06_sram_dma/ z80_stage06_bus_grant 8 src/stage08_virtual_io/ z80_stage08_virtual_io 9 src/stage09_flash_storage/ z80_stage09_flash_storage 9 automatic loader src/stage09_flash_storage/ z80_stage09_cpm_loader 10 src/stage10_websocket_terminal/ z80_stage10_websocket_terminal

Build the target in the table for your phase. Its UF2 is written to build/src/<source-directory-name>/<target>.uf2; for example, Phase 3 uses build/src/stage03_mcp23s17/z80_stage03_control_inputs.uf2.

docs.title: VS Code deployment options
docs.text:
Use Tasks: Run Task in the Z80ROMlessSBC workspace. Each implementation phase lists its Build Pico - … and Flash Pico - … tasks.

Phase Firmware task 9 Build and flash Pico - Phase 9 firmware 10 Build and flash Pico - Phase 10 firmware

Phase 9 prompts for Diagnostic or Automatic loader. Firmware tasks preserve disks and ENV settings. They force-update without checking the previous firmware. See task requirements. The commands below remain available for manual builds and provisioning.

docs.title: 7.1 Firmware and CP/M Build
docs.text:
The repository implements the cumulative phase firmware under src/. The former Phase 7 CPU fixture is now the Phase 6 bus-grant diagnostic; Phase 8-10 keep their existing numbers and target names. Phase 10 includes the journaled flash disks, CP/M boot loader, and WebSocket terminal. Its host build also assembles the board-native CP/M 2.2 BIOS, assembles the optimized CCP/BDOS from cpm64_z80.asm, and emits all provisionable images.

Install CMake, Ninja, Python 3.11 or newer, picotool, z80asm, and cpmtools (cpmcp and cpmrm install the native AUTORUN utility into drive A). See Toolchain for downloads, installation steps on macOS/Linux/Windows, runtime verification and platform-specific limits. The firmware needs a complete Arm GNU bare-metal toolchain with Newlib; the Homebrew compiler alone does not provide the required runtime. Install the Pico SDK with its Git submodules initialized. Run these commands from the repository root, replacing the SDK and toolchain paths with your local installations; the checked-in default SDK path is specific to the author's machine. A known working macOS setup is:

brew install cmake ninja picotool z80asm cpmtools
git submodule update --init --recursive
export PATH="$HOME/.local/share/arm-gnu-toolchain-15.3.rel1/bin:$PATH"
cmake -S . -B build -G Ninja \
  -DPICO_BOARD=pico2_w \
  -DPICO_SDK_PATH="$HOME/GitHub/pico/pico-sdk"
cmake --build build --target z80_stage01_supervisor -j

The VS Code firmware build tasks use scripts/pico_build.py to find a complete toolchain without pinning a release. It checks ARM_GNU_TOOLCHAIN_BIN first, then preserves the compiler in an existing build's CMake cache. For a new build, it searches PATH, skipping compilers without Newlib, followed by ~/.local/share/arm-gnu-toolchain*/bin (newest version first). It checks both the C and C++ runtime libraries. For another installation location, set ARM_GNU_TOOLCHAIN_BIN to its bin directory in the environment used to start VS Code. Changing an existing build's compiler requires a new build directory or an explicit cmake --fresh configure with the desired toolchain on PATH.

Phase 10 opens the unified system configuration shell over USB when Wi-Fi credentials are missing; Ctrl-] c opens it later. The old Ctrl-] n entry point is removed. SSID, password and the optional remote-FS IPv4 address are saved in the existing ENV store (WIFI_SSID, WIFI_PASSWORD, FS_SERVER). No credentials belong in CMake arguments or generated firmware headers. Until configured, CP/M and disk services continue over USB. The same shell configures OpenAI/Ollama chat, OpenWeatherMap and POSIX timezone settings. Quitting its main menu after saved changes announces a required reboot, flushes disks, safely stops the Z80, and reboots the Pico. Unchanged settings do not trigger a reboot. Save application work before quitting with changes. See the Phase 10 setup procedure. Remote-FS I/O remains deferred.

docs.title: Building from the Phase 1 directory
docs.text:
These source directories are not standalone CMake projects: they depend on the repository's top-level CMake configuration. cmake --build requires an already configured build tree; mkdir build alone does not create one. If it reports that the build directory is missing or that CMakeCache.txt is missing, run the configure step first.

To keep a local build tree while working in src/stage01_supervisor, run:

export PATH="$HOME/.local/share/arm-gnu-toolchain-15.3.rel1/bin:$PATH"
cmake -S ../.. -B build -G Ninja \
  -DPICO_BOARD=pico2_w \
  -DPICO_SDK_PATH="$HOME/GitHub/pico/pico-sdk"
cmake --build build --target z80_stage01_supervisor -j

As above, adjust the toolchain and SDK paths for your installation. Here, -S ../.. selects the repository root, while -B build writes the generated build tree inside the current source directory. The UF2 is therefore at src/stage01_supervisor/build/src/stage01_supervisor/z80_stage01_supervisor.uf2 relative to the repository root. Run subsequent build commands from the same source directory; root-level build and flashing examples elsewhere on this page assume a repository-root build/ tree instead.

docs.title: Building the full image set
docs.text:
The Phase 1 target builds the first hardware diagnostic. When you reach the storage/terminal phases, use the repository-root configuration above and run this from the repository root to build the full image set:

cmake --build build --target z80_cpm_images -j

The z80_cpm_images target builds Phase 10 and writes these files to build/cpm/:

Artifact Purpose z80boot.pkg Manifest, CRCs, and the reset-ready 64 KiB Z80 image drive_a_cpm63k-z80.img Native CP/M system disk with the Z80 SBC BIOS and native AUTORUN AUTORUN.COM Native auto-run configuration utility, also installed on drive A drive_b_bdsc.img through drive_d_blank.img Converted 320 KiB disks z80romless-flash.bin Complete 4 MiB initial-provisioning image manifest.json Geometry, addresses, sizes, and SHA-256 values

The native utility supports cold-only, warm-only, both, and disabled boot modes. Its settings use drive A's final reserved system record, not a CP/M file or boot-code location. Freshly generated drive A images initialize auto-run disabled. See native auto-run and recovery.

For the USB-only Phase 9 baseline, build this instead:

cmake --build build --target z80_stage09_cpm_images -j

It writes the same artifact names to build/cpm-stage09/, but the complete flash image contains Phase 9 firmware, not Phase 10. Phase 9 waits with RESET LOW until Ctrl+] l loads/verifies SRAM and Ctrl+] g starts at nominal 20 MHz. Its optional Ctrl+] t read-only Z80 disk test requires a reboot and fresh load before CP/M execution. See the Phase 9 USB workflow.

For normal operation without diagnostic load/start commands, build the separate automatic loader:

cmake --build build --target z80_stage09_cpm_loader -j

Its firmware is build/src/stage09_flash_storage/z80_stage09_cpm_loader.uf2. Every Pico reset recovers/validates storage, loads and verifies all SRAM, resets the Z80 and starts CP/M without requiring a connected terminal. Successful boot retains the CP/M banner/prompt for picocom and suppresses the diagnostic menu. The automatic-loader workflow documents startup, failure reporting and safe restart.

The optional z80_stage09_cpm_loader_images target emits the corresponding complete provisioning set in build/cpm-stage09-loader/.

Run the host regression checks with:

python3 -m unittest discover -s src/cpm -p 'test_*.py' -v

docs.title: Load phase firmware and open its console
docs.text:
1. Disconnect the bench supply and USB before changing installed devices. For initial Phase 1 loading, program the Pico off the breadboard so USB cannot energize untested wiring. Do this before fitting it and adding signal jumpers in Phase 1.
  2. Hold the Pico's BOOTSEL button while connecting its USB data cable to the computer, then release it. It appears as a removable drive in this mode, not as the application's serial port. BOOTSEL does not erase flash by itself.
  3. Load your phase's UF2 and reboot. The commands below are for Phase 1; for later phases, use the UF2 path for that phase from the table above.
  4. For initial Phase 1 setup, disconnect USB, fit the Pico, and complete the Phase 1 wiring checks with all power disconnected. Apply external +5 V before reconnecting USB, then open its USB serial port using a serial terminal. On macOS, inspect ls /dev/cu.usbmodem*; identify the port belonging to this Pico. No external USB-to-UART adapter is required.
  5. Select 115200 baud, 8 data bits, no parity, 1 stop bit, and no flow control if the terminal asks. This is USB CDC, so baud rate does not set Z80 clock speed. Commands are single characters, such as Phase 1 s for status and w for walking outputs; no Enter is required. Only one terminal program can use the port at a time.

For subsequent in-board programming, keep external +5 V applied before connecting USB and throughout programming. Disconnect USB before removing external +5 V. Do not program or run the populated board from USB alone: U9's AHCT245 data ports lack power-off isolation. Remove the Pico with both supplies disconnected if USB-only programming is needed.

Phase 1 programming commands for step 3, run from the repository root:

picotool load -v build/src/stage01_supervisor/z80_stage01_supervisor.uf2
picotool reboot

The port disappears during BOOTSEL/reboot and may get a different name when the application returns. Reconnect the terminal if needed. A missed startup banner is not a failed boot: try the phase's status command. If no port appears, first check that the cable carries data, the UF2 is for Pico 2 W, and the application has left BOOTSEL mode.

docs.title: macOS console with picocom
docs.text:
Install picocom once, then list the USB serial ports with the Pico running the phase firmware (not in BOOTSEL mode):

brew install picocom
ls /dev/cu.usbmodem*

Identify the port belonging to the Pico, then start the terminal, replacing the example device name with the one listed on your computer:

picocom --baud 115200 --databits 8 --parity n --stopbits 1 --flow n /dev/cu.usbmodemXXXX

Follow the power sequence above before connecting USB. Keep picocom open during console-driven tests. For Phase 1, type s to sample the inputs and w to run the control-output walking-one test; neither command needs Enter. Run w only with the required Phase 1 hardware population. To exit picocom, press Ctrl+A, then Ctrl+X. Close it before programming the Pico again or opening another terminal on the same port.

docs.title: 7.2 Flash Provisioning
docs.text:
Finish any running hardware test before provisioning

Building does not deploy. Do not replace firmware, open a second serial owner, or reset the Pico during an active soak. Disk/full-image replacement is destructive. This non-production development workflow creates no backups.

docs.title: Reusable Python flashing tools
docs.text:
Routine updates use scripts/pico_flash.py; standalone serial discovery and Phase 9 commands use scripts/pico_supervisor.py. Their complete setup, same-shell .venv-flash activation/preflight, examples, command options and troubleshooting now live under Tools: Pico flashing and USB supervisor.

For an already matching installation, follow the firmware-only update procedure. It confirms stop/flush, gracefully closes verified picocom owners, and verifies the programmed bytes without post-flash boot checks. Automatic stop speaks the currently running Phase 9 protocol; other running phases require their own safe stop before using --stopped.

docs.title: Selective disk updates without backups
docs.text: Use the selective disk procedure to replace only selected A-D slots without a firmware rebuild, backups or backup prompts. It includes native/Altair validation, Drive A compatibility checks, journal checks and read-back verification. Firmware, boot data, the journal, environment and unselected drives are not written.

docs.title: Full provisioning and coordinated system updates
docs.text:
Firmware-only updates leave the boot package, journal, persistent environment and all four disks unchanged. Do not overwrite Drive A or use a complete flash image merely to change startup mode. On new/disposable storage, build z80_stage09_cpm_loader_images and use its build/cpm-stage09-loader/z80romless-flash.bin instead of the manual image in the full-provisioning example below.

For Phase 9, build z80_stage09_cpm_images, enter BOOTSEL with the documented external-5-V-before-USB sequence, then provision new/disposable storage using:

picotool load -v build/cpm-stage09/z80romless-flash.bin -t bin -o 0x10000000
picotool reboot

To preserve drives B-D and the journal, selectively update the Phase 9 firmware, boot package and matching Drive A system image:

picotool load -v build/src/stage09_flash_storage/z80_stage09_flash_storage.uf2
picotool load -v build/cpm-stage09/z80boot.pkg -t bin -o 0x102A0000
picotool load -v build/cpm-stage09/drive_a_cpm63k-z80.img -t bin -o 0x102C0000
picotool reboot

Updating Drive A replaces its files; no backup is created by this workflow. Updating only the boot package leaves stale BIOS bytes in Drive A's reserved tracks and is not a complete matching-system update. Open USB CDC and follow the Phase 9 load/start procedure; no Wi-Fi credentials or browser are needed.

Before a selective disk-image update, complete a clean stop/flush. If a fault left a committed journal entry, recover and verify that old/new block first; do not let a pending replay overwrite part of a newly provisioned disk image.

The remaining examples provision the final Phase 10 network image. For a new or disposable flash, put the Pico in BOOTSEL mode and write the complete image. This erases existing CP/M disk contents, the journal and persistent environment variables:

picotool load -v build/cpm/z80romless-flash.bin -t bin -o 0x10000000
picotool reboot

For normal updates, load only the firmware and selected storage regions. These commands preserve regions not named by the input file:

picotool load -v build/src/stage10_websocket_terminal/z80_stage10_websocket_terminal.uf2
picotool load -v build/cpm/z80boot.pkg -t bin -o 0x102A0000
picotool load -v build/cpm/drive_a_cpm63k-z80.img -t bin -o 0x102C0000
picotool load -v build/cpm/drive_b_bdsc.img -t bin -o 0x10310000
picotool load -v build/cpm/drive_c_escape.img -t bin -o 0x10360000
picotool load -v build/cpm/drive_d_blank.img -t bin -o 0x103B0000
picotool reboot

After association, browse to http://<pico-dhcp-address>:8088/. The USB serial console reports Phase 10 startup and accepts s to print terminal queue/drop counts and disk/fatal status. CP/M disk writes are persistent; full reprovisioning replaces their contents without backups in this development workflow.

docs.title: Building and Testing Pico C Firmware
docs.text:
This is the complete software-validation workflow, from a fresh checkout to host tests, Z80 execution tests and deployable Pico firmware. Run commands from the repository root unless stated otherwise.

No Pico emulator is used

The Pico C logic runs natively on the development computer with test replacements for hardware-facing SDK calls. A separate emulator executes Z80 instructions, not the Pico firmware. Finally, the real ARM firmware is built against the real Pico SDK. These checks complement each other; none replaces testing the physical board.

docs.title: 1. Understand the four validation layers
docs.text:
Layer What runs What it establishes Native C/C++ host tests Maintained firmware logic compiled for the Mac or other host, with test SDK headers and functions Software state transitions, bounds, error handling and scripted fault/interleaving cases Independent Z80 execution Assembled Z80 programs, BIOS and CP/M in an instruction emulator, with modeled peripherals Actual Z80 instruction behavior, console/disk protocol use, boot and warm-boot behavior Pico cross-build ARM compiler and linker with the real Pico SDK Firmware compiles/links for Pico 2 W, SDK APIs are valid and artifacts fit the protected flash layout Physical bench qualification Deployed firmware, real Pico, Z80, SRAM, buffers and flash Actual USB behavior, multicore/interrupt operation, bus ownership, timing, electrical margins and sustained reliability

The host tests do not execute an ARM UF2 or emulate an RP2350. The Z80 tests do not execute the Pico C peripheral handlers: their peripherals are software models. A successful cross-build does not execute the firmware.

docs.title: 2. Prepare a fresh checkout and host tools
docs.text:
For a new checkout:

git clone https://github.com/gloveboxes/Z80ROMlessSBC.git
cd Z80ROMlessSBC
git submodule update --init --recursive

If already working in this repository, keep the existing checkout and changes. Do not clone over it or reset it to follow this guide.

On macOS, install Apple's Command Line Tools if not already installed:

xcode-select --install

With Homebrew available:

brew install cmake ninja python@3.14 z80asm
export PYTHON=python3.14
"$PYTHON" --version
cc --version
c++ --version

Python 3.11 or newer is required for the complete image/BIOS workflow; the commands use Python 3.14 as the tested macOS example. On another system, select an installed Python 3.11+ interpreter and install equivalent native C/C++ compilers, CMake, Ninja and z80asm. PYTHON is a shell convenience used by this guide, not a firmware CMake setting.

Node.js is optional for the browser-keyboard test. If it is installed, CMake adds terminal_keyboard; otherwise that test is not registered. Native firmware tests do not require npm dependency installation.

The native C tests need neither a Pico SDK nor an ARM toolchain. Both are needed later for the real firmware build.

docs.title: 3. Configure, build and run the native C tests
docs.text:
Use a separate build directory from the Pico cross-build. Explicitly select the host compilers, not arm-none-eabi-gcc:

cmake -S src/common/tests -B build/host-control -G Ninja \
  -DCMAKE_C_COMPILER=cc \
  -DCMAKE_CXX_COMPILER=c++
cmake --build build/host-control
ctest --test-dir build/host-control --output-on-failure --no-tests=error

The HTTP file-transfer tests exercise the production parser and port 21/22 handshake, binary data, files larger than 64 KiB, framing errors, EOF, cancellation, stale DNS callbacks and TCP backpressure. The async transport regression covers consecutive TLS receive callbacks before the worker runs, a full 16 KiB record, incremental freeing during a 70 KB stream, backlog overflow, and stage-specific timeout diagnostics. The test with the actual Mbed TLS configuration enforces a TCP window large enough for an input record and framing overhead. These tests run offline. To also build the optional live runner with the firmware's real Mbed TLS configuration and trust bundle, configure with PICO_SDK_PATH:

cmake -S src/common/tests -B build/host-control -G Ninja \
  -DCMAKE_C_COMPILER=cc -DCMAKE_CXX_COMPILER=c++ \
  -DPICO_SDK_PATH=/absolute/path/to/pico-sdk
cmake --build build/host-control --target http_live_test
python3 src/common/tests/http_transfer_integration.py \
  --runner build/host-control/http_live_test --https

The script starts temporary local Python HTTP servers, transfers a 76,805-byte binary, an empty file, a redirect and a chunked response, checks 404 failure, and rejects an untrusted local HTTPS certificate. --https additionally transfers the supplied GitHub LOVE.BAS through verified TLS 1.2 and compares every byte with an independent HTTPS fetch. It needs network access and the openssl CLI. The native socket adapter tests the production FT driver, parser and crypto; the separate async transport regression covers the Pico lwIP adapter. These checks do not flash hardware or prove board timing.

This configures a standalone host CMake project. Its test targets enable warnings as errors and keep assertions enabled with -UNDEBUG, including when the build type would normally disable assertions.

The equivalent existing convenience command is npm run test:control. It configures, builds and runs the native suite; it does not provision an emulator environment or deploy to hardware.

docs.title: What replaces the hardware?
docs.text:
Test headers live in src/common/tests/fakes/. Each harness supplies the functions needed by the production code under test. Depending on the test, these include:

Hardware/SDK operation Host test implementation Flash access through XIP (execute-in-place mapping) A 4 MiB byte array Flash erase/program Modeled sector/page operations, alignment/bounds checks and flash programming bit rules Assisted Z80 SRAM access A 64 KiB array, or an injected-cycle model in the loader/control tests GPIO, reset and clock control Recorded pin/control state, expected operations or requested frequencies Time and deadlines Controlled software time rather than a measured real-time clock Watchdog reboot An intercepted reboot, followed by simulated restart/recovery using the retained flash array USB CDC input/output Controlled connection state, input bytes and output capacity Core/queue interaction Test queues and explicitly scripted ordering; not a real RP2350 dual-core execution

The replacements differ between harnesses. A stubbed helper passing a test is not proof of that helper's real SDK implementation.

docs.title: Phase 9 coverage and its boundaries
docs.text:
CTest name Maintained code exercised Important boundary flash_backend_recovery Actual flash_backend.c: manifest validation, byte loading/readback controller, cache, journal programming and recovery Flash, SRAM byte access, bus/clock calls and reboot are modeled stage09_usb_cpm Actual Phase 9 application functions and shared terminal_queue.c Boot/storage and SDK calls are substituted; command/stop interleavings are driven by the harness usb_core1_console Actual usb_console.c routing and bounded diagnostic ring Modeled SDK endpoints assert core-1 affinity; checks concurrent producer/drain, CRLF vs raw console bytes, backpressure, wrap, overflow, disconnect and init failure, not physical IRQ delivery stage09_autoboot_cpm The same application compiled with automatic startup, including its actual main initialization path SDK/storage calls are substituted; tests cover boot before USB connection, retained CP/M output, late failure reporting and no automatic retries disk_protocol Actual disk_device.c: Z80-facing commands, queues, BUSY publication and fatal error latch The flash backend is stubbed; this is not the journal test assisted_loader, control_faults Shared injected-loader and control code Cycle/pin models do not establish physical setup/hold timing

The flash-backend test injects bad package lengths/CRCs/reset vectors, cancelled loads, SRAM read/write/mismatch faults, corrupt journal programming and all eight supported watchdog fault points. The terminal test checks framing, ordinary CP/M input, queue/backpressure behavior, startup reports, safe stop and a 20 MHz start request. That last check does not generate or measure a 20 MHz signal. The application harness also checks deferred supervisor commands, queue-full rejection, early core-1 startup, disk-first ordering, USB service while workers are disabled or paused, and fail-closed initialization. USB endpoint fakes reject any call from core 0; CPU-control fakes reject calls from core 1. The SDK alarm/USB IRQ affinity still needs verification on the board.

For a focused native Phase 9 run:

cmake --build build/host-control \
  --target flash_backend_test stage09_test stage09_autoboot_test disk_test
ctest --test-dir build/host-control \
  -R '^(flash_backend_recovery|stage09_usb_cpm|stage09_autoboot_cpm|disk_protocol)$' \
  --output-on-failure --no-tests=error

The authoritative target/test list is src/common/tests/CMakeLists.txt.

docs.title: 4. Add the independent Z80 instruction emulator
docs.text:
This is an optional host-only dependency, separate from the Pico SDK. The environment name is shared with the existing arithmetic/SRAM soak tests. Create it once; reuse it if already configured:

"$PYTHON" -m venv build/math-soak-emulator
build/math-soak-emulator/bin/python -m pip install \
  -r src/common/tests/requirements-soak.txt

The requirements pin z80==1.0.0. Register that interpreter with the native test project and rebuild:

cmake -S src/common/tests -B build/host-control -G Ninja \
  -DCMAKE_C_COMPILER=cc \
  -DCMAKE_CXX_COMPILER=c++ \
  -DSOAK_EMULATOR_PYTHON="$PWD/build/math-soak-emulator/bin/python"
cmake --build build/host-control
ctest --test-dir build/host-control -N \
  -R '^(math_soak_z80_execution|scope_z80_execution|cpm_bios_z80_execution)$'

The listing must contain all three named execution tests. Without SOAK_EMULATOR_PYTHON, those tests are not registered; passing the remaining native suite does not imply they ran. --no-tests=error rejects an empty selection, but does not detect a partly missing selection: inspect the names.

Run the execution tests:

ctest --test-dir build/host-control \
  -R '^(math_soak_z80_execution|scope_z80_execution|cpm_bios_z80_execution)$' \
  --output-on-failure --no-tests=error

The actual resident Z80 math/scope images run in the independent core. The CP/M execution test assembles the maintained BIOS and CCP/BDOS, then checks cold boot, BIOS reports, directories on A-D, transient exit/warm boot, and all 10,240 records of the read-only disk diagnostic. Software peripheral models provide terminal and disk responses. This verifies instructions and protocol use, not Pico interrupt latency or USB/flash hardware timing.

For a focused Phase 9 run with emulation enabled:

ctest --test-dir build/host-control \
  -R '^(flash_backend_recovery|stage09_usb_cpm|stage09_autoboot_cpm|disk_protocol|cpm_bios_z80_execution)$' \
  --output-on-failure --no-tests=error

Expect five named CTest checks; the CP/M execution check contains multiple Python test cases. The host environment never opens the board's USB port.

docs.title: 5. Validate CP/M image construction
docs.text:
With Python 3.11+ and z80asm available:

"$PYTHON" -m unittest discover -s src/cpm -p 'test_*.py' -v

These image tests check packaging, CRCs, exact memory/disk geometry, BIOS jump-table compatibility and CP/M translation. They are not the independent instruction-execution tests above.

The separate project-owned CP/M host also tests multi-extent programs and cross-drive writes; see the end-to-end CP/M procedure for its build and run commands. Neither host model replaces the Pico/physical-board gate.

docs.title: 6. Cross-compile the real Pico firmware
docs.text:
Follow Toolchain for host prerequisites and complete Arm compiler installation before configuring a firmware build.

Install a complete Arm GNU bare-metal toolchain for your host, including Newlib. Select the arm-none-eabi toolchain; a compiler without its C runtime is insufficient. The example path below matches the tested local installation; adjust it to your installed version.

Install the Pico SDK with submodules if it is not already present:

mkdir -p "$HOME/GitHub/pico"
git clone --recurse-submodules https://github.com/raspberrypi/pico-sdk.git \
  "$HOME/GitHub/pico/pico-sdk"

Reuse an existing complete SDK instead of cloning over it. On macOS, picotool can be installed with brew install picotool. Then configure the separate firmware build:

export PATH="$HOME/.local/share/arm-gnu-toolchain-15.3.rel1/bin:$PATH"
arm-none-eabi-gcc --version
arm-none-eabi-gcc -print-file-name=libc.a
cmake -S . -B build/pico -G Ninja \
  -DPICO_BOARD=pico2_w \
  -DPICO_SDK_PATH="$HOME/GitHub/pico/pico-sdk" \
  -DPython3_EXECUTABLE="$(command -v "$PYTHON")"
cmake --build build/pico \
  --target z80_stage09_cpm_images z80_stage09_cpm_loader_images z80_cpm_images

If the Newlib query prints only libc.a rather than a library path, check the toolchain installation. Initial configuration also needs network access to obtain the pinned WebSocket dependency if it is not cached.

This builds both Phase 9 variants and Phase 10 against the real SDK. Empty Wi-Fi credentials keep networking disabled; credentials are not needed for the Phase 9 USB baseline. For network testing, configure credentials locally without sharing generated headers or CMake caches.

Output under build/pico/ Purpose src/stage09_flash_storage/z80_stage09_flash_storage.uf2 Deployable Phase 9 Pico firmware src/stage09_flash_storage/z80_stage09_cpm_loader.uf2 Automatic Phase 9 loader, independent of USB connection src/stage10_websocket_terminal/z80_stage10_websocket_terminal.uf2 Deployable Phase 10 Pico firmware cpm-stage09/ Matching Phase 9 boot package, disks, manifest and complete flash image cpm-stage09-loader/ Matching automatic-loader provisioning set cpm/ Matching Phase 10 provisioning set

The build generates UF2/binary images; it does not flash or execute them. The firmware variants retain their distinct clock configuration: Phase 9 uses 20 MHz after complete load/verification, either on explicit commands or automatically on reset with the loader variant, while Phase 10 retains its separate 1 MHz startup default. Neither is qualified by a build. The linker protects storage above firmware offset 0x290000; the physical flash size remains 4 MiB.

Use the firmware build/provisioning reference for other phase firmware targets and verified provisioning commands. Use matching boot-package and Drive A system images after BIOS changes. Full-flash provisioning replaces all disk contents; keep backups.

docs.title: 7. Record software results, then qualify the board
docs.text:
Record the source revision/local changes, tool versions, build configuration, test names/results and artifact hashes. Keep separate labels for:

  • Host logic tests passed.
  • Z80 instruction-emulator tests passed.
  • Real Pico firmware cross-build passed.
  • Physical bench tests passed at the recorded measured clock.

Do not collapse these into an unqualified "hardware passed". Native tests do not establish real dual-core scheduling, SDK flash lockout, interrupt/trap latency, USB enumeration/backpressure, actual reset/BUSACK transitions, electrical margins or flash endurance.

Do not disturb an active physical test

No software check above requires opening serial, resetting or programming the board. Leave an existing soak and its serial owner alone. Wait for it to finish before deploying; do not change probes or wiring while running.

After software validation, follow the Phase 9 controlled USB workflow and its bench checklist. Observe the CP/M prompt and filesystem behavior, verify safe stop/recovery, and collect the required frequency/timing evidence. The Z80 clock has been scope-measured at 20 MHz on the project breadboard. Integrated CP/M, disk-I/O and receiving-pin timing checks remain separate qualification evidence.

docs.title: I/O Ports and Services
docs.text:
The Pico provides virtual peripherals through Z80 IN and OUT instructions. This page owns the port allocation and the ROMLESS-SVC/1 extended-service protocol, compatible with the ESP32 Altair io_ports.h and dcc DXSVC.H client. Extended services are implemented in both Phase 9 variants and Phase 10. Phase 8 retains its original bring-up diagnostics.

Maintained sources: transport and timers, service worker, clock and utilities, persistent environment store and public constants. See operational boundaries for the terminal, disk and clock-stop trap contracts.

docs.title: Port allocation
docs.text:
The four monitored address bits, A0/A1/A2/A4, provide 16 distinct ports: 0x00-0x07 and 0x10-0x17, using address & 0x17. Other addresses are aliases, not additional ports. For example, 0x08 aliases 0x00 and 0x18 aliases 0x10. No additional wiring is required.

Port (hex) Decimal Function Allocation 0x00 0 Terminal data, IN/OUT Fixed 0x01 1 Terminal status Fixed 0x02 2 Shared service command (OUT) / status (IN) Implemented 0x03 3 Shared service length-prefixed request bytes (OUT) Implemented 0x04 4 Shared service length-prefixed response bytes (IN) Implemented 0x05 5 BIOS cold-entry/CCP-handoff reports; Phase 9 disk-test and Phase 10 qualification results Reserved for diagnostics 0x06 6 Phase 9 disk-test bytes and Phase 10 qualification data; Phase 8 test results Reserved for diagnostics 0x07 7 Spare; ESP32 interrupt timer is deferred on this hardware Unallocated 0x10 16 Disk command (OUT) / status (IN) Fixed 0x11 17 Disk drive selection Fixed 0x12 18 Disk sector address, low byte Fixed 0x13 19 Disk sector address, high byte Fixed 0x14 20 Disk data, IN/OUT Fixed 0x15 21 HTTP(S) file-transfer command (OUT) / status (IN) Implemented in Phase 10 0x16 22 File-transfer filename/data bytes Implemented in Phase 10 0x17 23 Independent countdown timers and stopwatches, IN/OUT Implemented

This assigns or reserves 15 ports and leaves one spare. A port supports both IN and OUT, so a command and its status can share one number.

The BIOS emits B0h on port 0x05 at cold entry and C0h immediately before handoff to CCP (including warm boot). Phase 9 observes these as execution milestones, not proof of a working CP/M prompt. Its read-only disk test uses port 0x06 for compared bytes and 5Ah/E1h on port 0x05 for completion/ failure. These diagnostic meanings are mode-specific and do not change the fixed terminal or disk ABI.

docs.title: HTTP and HTTPS file transfer
docs.text:
Phase 10 implements the existing FT.ASM port protocol without changing the application. Use the existing FT.COM, or assemble the original source with CP/M MAC FT followed by LOAD FT. The network uses standard HTTP/1.1 GET requests; a Python-specific file server and HTTP Range support are unnecessary. Phase 9 exposes the same ports but returns ERROR for downloads because it has no network backend.

The driver accepts a full http:// or https:// URL, or a filename relative to persistent HTTP_BASE_URL. A relative filename extends the base path; a name starting with / uses the server's root. The base must have no query. Settings are reloaded on core 1 at the first GET of each new transfer.

CP/M uppercases command tails. Use the interactive ENV editor (run ENV without arguments, then A to add, or the entry number to edit) to preserve the case of URL paths. Set the key to HTTP_BASE_URL and its value to:

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/AzureSphereCloudEnabledAltair8800/RetroGames/refs/heads/main/

Quit ENV with Q, then download and run the supplied BASIC example:

FT -G LOVE.BAS
MBASIC LOVE

-G retains FT's existing text behavior: normalize line endings to CR LF and append CP/M's ^Z marker. Use FT -GB PROGRAM.COM for byte-preserving binary transfers. FT saves the basename using CP/M's uppercase 8.3 naming and pads the final 128-byte disk record with NULs. If the remote filename is omitted, run FT -G or FT -GB; FT prompts for a case-preserving remote path and derives the local uppercase basename. This supports mixed-case HTTP paths while keeping the CCP command-tail behavior unchanged.

For a local server, run this on the host in the directory containing files:

python3 -m http.server 8000 --bind 0.0.0.0

In interactive ENV, change HTTP_BASE_URL to the host's LAN address, for example http://192.168.1.10:8000/, then use FT -G LOVE.BAS or FT -GB PROGRAM.COM. For mixed-case server paths, omit the filename and enter it at FT's prompt. Plain HTTP works without synchronized calendar time.

HTTPS requires Wi-Fi and synchronized SNTP time, and verifies certificate dates, hostname (with SNI), and chain. The default trust bundle contains ISRG Root X1, USERTrust RSA Certification Authority and GTS Root R4. For a different public/private CA, configure the firmware with -DZ80_HTTP_CA_FILE=/absolute/path/to/bundle.pem, retaining any roots you still need. Self-signed/untrusted servers fail; verification is never disabled.

The dedicated http_io.c driver provides this ABI, independently of framed services on ports 2/3/4:

Operation Behavior OUT 21, 1 Reset transfer; collect a new filename/URL OUT 22, byte Append filename bytes, terminated by NUL OUT 21, 3 Request the next chunk; status becomes BUSY IN 21 0 IDLE, 1 DATA, 2 EOF, 3 BUSY, 4 missing/empty HTTP_BASE_URL, 255 ERROR IN 22 Read the count (0 means 256), then exactly that many file bytes OUT 21, 4 Close/cancel and return to IDLE

DATA remains visible until the entire chunk is consumed, including the final partial chunk. Empty files report EOF without a count byte. Repeated GET commands while busy or while unread data remains do not duplicate requests. SET_FILENAME and CLOSE invalidate pending work; late responses and DNS answers cannot become part of a new file. Reset the transfer to recover after ERROR. For relative filenames, status 4 means HTTP_BASE_URL is missing or empty; FT prints instructions for adding or editing it in ENV. Absolute HTTP/HTTPS URLs do not need this setting.

Core 0 only handles bounded port operations and a release/acquire mailbox. Core 1 owns ENV reads, DNS, TCP/TLS, HTTP parsing and a 1024-byte ring. One GET stream supplies 256-byte FT chunks; files need not fit in RAM. Network writes and receive parsing are limited to 512 bytes per poll. A bounded chain of lwIP receive buffers and deferred TCP credit apply backpressure when FT stops reading, while the worker continues servicing disks, USB and the terminal. Consumed buffer prefixes are freed on each poll, so the backlog stays bounded as the file grows. Successive decrypted TLS fragments are accepted together, including a final fragment followed by TLS close notification. The receive bound is the TCP window plus one TLS input record (33,904 bytes); exceeding it fails explicitly. The client also registers lwIP's half-second poll callback to advance buffered TLS work after temporary memory pressure.

The TCP receive window is 17,520 bytes, enough for Mbed TLS's 16 KiB input record and framing overhead. A smaller window can stall TLS before plaintext is available to acknowledge. A compile-time check and the native test with the real crypto configuration enforce this size relationship. The existing pbuf pool and lwIP heap sizes are unchanged.

HTTP transfer diagnostics are kept off the serial console. Transfer failures remain available through the FT status response.

The parser accepts HTTP/1.0 and 1.1, content-length, chunked (including trailers), and connection-close bodies, preserving binary NULs. It rejects truncated framed responses, conflicting lengths, unsupported compression and HTTP errors. Up to five redirects are followed, including relative locations; HTTPS-to-HTTP downgrades fail. DNS names/IPv4 and optional ports are supported; IPv6, credentials, fragments and control characters are rejected. Filename/URL and path buffers allow 767 bytes, hostnames 253, header lines 1023, and each header or trailer section 8192. The unchanged FT application has CP/M's shorter 127-byte command-tail limit. A network stall times out after 30 seconds; waiting on a retained receive chain due to consumer backpressure is exempt.

docs.title: Interpreting CP/M SURVEY results
docs.text:
On the earlier Phase 9 USB CP/M loader, before extended services, SURVEY (System Survey, June 1982) reported 111 active ports. This was the alias set of the seven terminal/disk registers, not 111 independent peripherals.

Because A3 and A5-A7 are ignored, each register has 16 equivalent addresses within the low-byte range 0x00-0xFF. For example, 0x01, 0x09, 0x21 and 0x29 all access terminal status; 0x10, 0x18, 0x30 and 0x38 all access disk command/status. Seven registers occupy 112 low-byte addresses; the captured scan omitted 0x00, leaving 111.

Extended services add readable registers, so a new scan need not reproduce that historical count. An active result does not prove correct peripheral operation. Scanning the response port can also cause an explicit UNDERFLOW error; RESET the shared channel before using it afterward.

docs.title: Why A4 is monitored but A3 is not
docs.text:
The Pico decodes I/O ports using address & 0x17. The & operator is bitwise AND: a result bit is 1 only when both corresponding bits are 1. The hexadecimal mask 0x17 is binary 0001 0111:

Address bit:  A7 A6 A5 A4 A3 A2 A1 A0
Mask 0x17:     0  0  0  1  0  1  1  1

This keeps A4, A2, A1 and A0, matching the four address connections to U7. A3, A5-A7 and the high address byte are deliberately ignored for I/O decoding.

Address 0x08:  0000 1000
Mask    0x17:  0001 0111
               ---------
AND result:    0000 0000 = 0x00

Thus 0x08 aliases 0x00, 0x09 aliases 0x01, and 0xFF aliases the timer port 0x17. A4 distinguishes console 0x00/01 from disk 0x10-14. With a mask of 0x07, disk command 0x10 would incorrectly alias console data. Service group 0x30 is a byte written to command port 0x02, not an OUT to physical port 0x30 (which aliases disk command 0x10).

This omission applies only to I/O monitoring, not memory addressing. A3 still connects Z80 pin 33 to SRAM pin 9 in Phase 4; do not connect it to U7.

docs.title: Framing and recovery
docs.text:
There is one outstanding shared transaction at a time:

  1. Write RESET (0x01) to port 0x02 to recover an unknown parser state.
  2. Write the service group to 0x02.
  3. Write a 16-bit little-endian payload length to 0x03, then that many payload bytes. Length includes the operation byte and must be 1-2048.
  4. Poll status on 0x02 with a bounded client-side polling limit.
  5. For RESPONSE_READY, read the 16-bit little-endian response length from 0x04, then exactly that many bytes. The last byte returns the channel to READY. An empty response still has its two length bytes.
  6. For COMPLETE, write ACK (0x00) to 0x02.
  7. For ERROR, read the length prefix and one-byte error code from 0x04, then ACK. If an overlapping transaction poisoned the parser, RESET is required instead.
Status Value Meaning READY 0x00 Can accept a new command COMPLETE 0x01 Successful operation with no response; ACK required RESPONSE_READY 0x02 Length-prefixed response can be read COLLECTING 0x03 Awaiting the length prefix or remaining payload BUSY 0x04 Worker executing the request ERROR 0xFF Length-prefixed error can be read

Special commands on 0x02 are ACK (0x00), RESET (0x01) and IDENTIFY (0x02). IDENTIFY needs no request and returns the text ROMLESS-SVC/1 with the usual response length prefix. Text replies have no trailing NUL; binary replies are not strings.

RESET invalidates pending replies through a generation identifier, but does not undo side effects or cancel a worker already writing flash. A new worker request can return BUSY_ERROR until that job finishes. RESET does not reset running timers or stopwatches. There is no automatic server timeout for an incomplete request: the client must use bounded polling, report failure and RESET. Reading status never acknowledges COMPLETE.

docs.title: Bounded trap work
docs.text:
Phases 9/10 dispatch the already-masked port directly to the terminal, disk or extended-service handler. Terminal and disk requests do not probe the list of extended-service ports. Adding service groups behind 0x02-0x04 therefore does not add dispatch checks to those existing hot paths.

Core 0 reads a completed worker response in place instead of copying its payload during the status trap. The worker's result stays unchanged until core 0 submits another job; the parser must consume or discard the response before that submission. Errors, IDENTIFY and local timer replies use a separate small buffer. RESET still invalidates stale worker generations. This removes up to 2048 copied bytes from a completion trap and the separate 2048-byte response array; it does not remove the bounded request copy at submission or change the one-outstanding-transaction protocol.

Native regressions check zero response-payload copying for lengths 0, 1, 16 and 2048, response lifetime, framing, RESET, errors, and terminal/disk dispatch without service probes. These are work-count and correctness checks, not measurements of Z80 throughput or worst-case trap latency. Clock handover, data-path settling, disk-first worker scheduling and regular network polling are unchanged; hardware before/after measurements remain necessary.

Error codes match the ESP32 client:

Code Error 0x01 / 0x02 UNKNOWN_GROUP / UNKNOWN_OPERATION 0x03 / 0x04 INVALID_LENGTH / INVALID_PARAMETER 0x05 / 0x06 UNAVAILABLE / BUSY_ERROR 0x07 / 0x08 / 0x09 TIMEOUT (reserved) / INVALID_STATE / UNDERFLOW 0x10 / 0x11 / 0x12 STORAGE_OPEN / STORAGE_READ / STORAGE_WRITE 0x13 / 0x14 CAPACITY / NOT_FOUND 0x15 / 0x16 CLOCK_UNSYNCED / REBOOT_CONFIRMATION

docs.title: Groups and operations
docs.text:
All integer request fields and binary results are little-endian.

Group Operations and payloads Result Timers 0x10 [0, id, duration_u32] starts/replaces; [1, id] queries COMPLETE or one byte, 1 running / 0 expired Stopwatches 0x11 [0, id] resets; [1, id] reads seconds; [2, id] reads milliseconds COMPLETE or unsigned 32-bit elapsed count Clock 0x20 [0] uptime seconds; [1] UTC ISO 8601; [2] local ISO 8601; [3] long local date; [4] DATE-style local date/time Text Utility 0x21 [0] random; [1, selector] system info; [2, 0xA5] confirmed reboot; [3] version; [4, state] set onboard LED; [5] read LED state Two random bytes, text, COMPLETE, or one LED-state byte Environment 0x30 Operations below Text or COMPLETE Weather 0x40 [0, field_id] reads text; [1] reads status Phase 10 cached weather; Phase 9 UNAVAILABLE Chat 0x50 Reset/append/submit/status/chunk operations below Phase 10 streaming OpenAI/Ollama; Phase 9 UNAVAILABLE Sense HAT 0x60 Recognized group without a Pico driver UNAVAILABLE

There are four countdown timers: IDs 0-2 take 0-65535 milliseconds; ID 3 takes 0-255 whole seconds. The shared duration field is four bytes for client compatibility, but out-of-range values are rejected. Timer 3 uses the ESP32 whole-second boundary rule: (current_ms / 1000 + duration) * 1000. A zero duration expires immediately.

There are three stopwatches, IDs 0-2. Reads do not reset them. A latched 32-bit millisecond count wraps after about 49.7 days; seconds wrap after about 136 years. Internal deadlines and uptime use a 64-bit monotonic clock.

Phase 10 starts SNTP against pool.ntp.org after Wi-Fi association. Calendar operations return CLOCK_UNSYNCED until the first valid synchronization. Phase 9 has no network time source and returns CLOCK_UNSYNCED for calendar queries. Uptime remains available in both. Local formatting uses persistent TZ in POSIX timezone syntax (for example, AEST-10); an absent TZ means UTC.

docs.title: CLOCK application time compatibility
docs.text:
The ESP32 Altair dcc Apps/CLOCK time interface is already provided by these services; no extra physical ports or separate time driver are needed:

CLOCK request Pico interface Result Local time Clock group 0x20, payload [2] on shared ports 2/3/4 YYYY-MM-DDTHH:MM:SS (19 bytes) Local date Clock group 0x20, payload [3] Monday, 01 January 2024 Uptime Clock group 0x20, payload [0] Decimal seconds since Pico startup Start refresh timer OUT 23: 0x12, 50, 0 Timer 2, 50 ms, low duration byte first Query refresh timer OUT 23: 0x22, then IN 23 1 while running, 0 when expired

The timer port remains usable while a shared clock request is BUSY. Calendar formatting, ENV access, and network time synchronization run on core 1; the Z80 trap only transfers the framed request/reply or handles the independent monotonic timer. Calendar replies contain exactly their length-prefixed text, without a trailing NUL.

For Phase 10, connect Wi-Fi and allow DNS/UDP access to pool.ntp.org. Calendar requests return explicit CLOCK_UNSYNCED (0x15) errors until SNTP has supplied a valid time. Once synchronized, time continues advancing from the monotonic clock through Wi-Fi outages and is corrected by later SNTP updates. Uptime and the refresh timer do not depend on Wi-Fi or SNTP.
