Configure the timezone through the existing ENV service, for example ENV TZ=AEST-10 for UTC+10 or ENV TZ=ACST-9:30 for UTC+09:30. POSIX signs are opposite to conventional UTC offsets. A full POSIX TZ rule can include daylight-saving transitions. Changes take effect on the next clock request without rebooting. The Pico remains TZ-only: the ESP32 CLOCK help text's UTC_OFFSET setting is not used here.

The unchanged CLOCK source also polls the weather group on every refresh. Phase 10 now supplies its cached status and field requests through the weather service. Phase 9 remains USB-only and returns UNAVAILABLE for weather.

The clock_app_time_services host integration test drives CLOCK's port transactions through the real parser, worker, calendar formatter, SNTP callback hook, and persistent ENV backend. It covers unsynchronized errors, UTC/local/date/uptime shapes, timezone updates and DST, 50 ms timer operation during a BUSY request, and the 32-bit millisecond rollover. It does not execute the CLOCK binary or qualify physical network/hardware operation.

docs.title: CHAT application: OpenAI and Ollama
docs.text:
Phase 10 implements the framed ABI used by the ESP32 Altair dcc Apps/CHAT/CHATC11.C application. Use the existing CP/M application and its CHAT.SYS system-prompt file; no BIOS, pin or disk-layout change is needed. CHAT 1.7-c11 adds application-side thinking control as described below; earlier versions still work but leave thinking at the server default. Firmware builds do not install the application on a disk. Do not use the legacy physical chat ports 120-124: they alias unrelated peripherals with this board's address decoding.

All requests use group 0x50 through shared ports 2/3/4:

Payload Result [0] Cancel any previous request and clear request assembly; COMPLETE [1, json_bytes...] Append 1-2047 bytes; COMPLETE, or explicit CAPACITY/BUSY/invalid-input error [2] Cancel the connection and clear queued response/error text; COMPLETE; assembled request is retained [3] Submit the assembled request asynchronously; COMPLETE, or BUSY/empty-request error [4] One status byte: 0 EOF, 1 WAITING, 2 DATA_READY [5, maximum_u16] [status, count_u16, text_bytes...], with status after removing the returned bytes

maximum is 1-2045, bounded by the 2048-byte service payload. CHATC11 requests 256 bytes at a time and appends JSON in 2047-byte pieces. The assembled request limit is 8191 bytes, excluding its local NUL terminator. Overflow never silently truncates a request. Appending or resubmitting while active returns BUSY. Operation 0 cancels before reusing the request buffer, so a new turn recovers safely after CHATC11 fills its local response buffer or times out. Operation 2 also cancels immediately. Shared transport RESET only invalidates the mailbox reply; as with ENV, it does not undo service side effects.

docs.title: Provider configuration
docs.text:
For a local Ollama server with its OpenAI-compatible API:

ENV CHAT_PROVIDER=compatible
ENV CHAT_ENDPOINT=http://192.168.1.26:11434/v1/chat/completions
ENV -I CHAT_MODEL=phi4-mini:3.8b
ENV CHAT_MAX_TOKENS=1024
ENV CHAT_TEMPERATURE=0.7

With CHAT 1.7-c11, CHAT_THINK defaults to false for CHAT_PROVIDER=compatible or ollama. The application sends "reasoning_effort":"none" to request a direct answer. Set ENV CHAT_THINK=true to send "reasoning_effort":"medium" (thinking on for boolean-control models, medium effort where supported), or ENV CHAT_THINK=default to omit the field and use the server/model default. Only models that support disabling thinking can honor none.

The USB configuration shell also edits this setting: Ctrl-] c, then 3 - Chat, then 7 - configure thinking. Enter false, true or default; - clears the key to the app's false default. Like other saved configuration changes, exiting the shell triggers a safe reboot.

The app re-reads provider/thinking settings before each turn and never adds the parameter to OpenAI requests. Invalid values or ENV errors stop submission explicitly. An absent/empty thinking value is seeded as false on first use; the standard service helper can print NOT_FOUND while seeding a missing key. Other compatible servers that do not support reasoning_effort should use CHAT_THINK=default to retain their old request format. Installing the updated CHAT.COM is required for this behavior; the existing Pico firmware needs no change and continues to forward the application's bounded JSON unchanged.

CHAT_PROVIDER=ollama is an alias for compatible. Discover installed model names from a host with curl http://192.168.1.26:11434/api/tags; the model must match a deployed name exactly. CHATC11's built-in gemma3:1b default is not guaranteed to be installed. The example server address is configuration, not a compiled-in endpoint.

For OpenAI:

ENV CHAT_PROVIDER=openai
ENV -I CHAT_OPENAI_KEY=<your-api-key>
ENV -I CHAT_MODEL=gpt-4o-mini
ENV CHAT_MAX_TOKENS=1024
ENV CHAT_TEMPERATURE=0.7

The ENV CLI evaluates +/- inside ordinary assignments as arithmetic. Use literal -I for API keys and model names; it only inserts absent keys. To replace an existing key, first use ENV -D CHAT_MODEL (or ENV -D CHAT_OPENAI_KEY), then its literal insert command. Do not paste real keys into logs or source control. ENV is plaintext onboard flash, not encrypted secret storage.

An absent provider defaults to openai. OpenAI always uses https://api.openai.com/v1/chat/completions, ignoring CHAT_ENDPOINT. Only OpenAI requests carry CHAT_OPENAI_KEY; a saved OpenAI key is never forwarded to an Ollama/compatible endpoint. Authenticated third-party compatible providers are not supported. URLs require an explicit path and accept HTTP or HTTPS, a DNS name/IPv4 address, and an optional port 1-65535. User-info, fragments, whitespace and control characters are rejected. Limits are 95 host bytes, 103 authority bytes, 159 path bytes, and 255 key bytes.

Core 1 reloads provider/endpoint/key from durable ENV on each submission. CHATC11 owns the JSON model, history, system prompt, token count, temperature and thinking parameter; restart CHAT after changing model/token/temperature settings. Thinking/provider changes are read at the next turn by CHAT 1.7-c11. HTTPS requires synchronized SNTP time and verifies certificate dates, chain and hostname using the bundled GTS Root R4. There is no insecure TLS fallback. Compatible HTTPS endpoints need a chain trusted by that root; arbitrary private/self-signed CAs are not supported. Plain HTTP Ollama works without SNTP but must remain on a trusted LAN.

docs.title: Ownership, bounds and failure behavior
docs.text:
The trap transfers framed bytes through the existing release/acquire atomic single-request mailbox. It does not access ENV, JSON, sockets or TLS, and never waits for an answer from the provider. Core 1 owns request assembly, the 4096-byte response ring, configuration, and the independent async HTTP client. Wi-Fi, terminal sessions and chat do not consume one another's queues or configure one another. Disk work still runs first on every application loop.

HTTP writes and received wire processing are limited to 512 bytes per service pass. A received pbuf chain is retained without extra copying, bounded to one chain of at most 16 KiB; further chains receive lwIP ERR_MEM backpressure. TCP credit advances only for bytes consumed by the parser. A full CP/M response ring pauses parsing rather than dropping text or blocking the other services. Accepted TCP writes are never replayed after a failed flush. Callback teardown is deferred to the service loop, callbacks are detached before abort, and generation tokens reject stale DNS/connection callbacks after cancellation.

The decoder accepts HTTP/1.0 or 1.1, content-length, connection-close or chunked bodies, and OpenAI-style single-line SSE JSON records. It requires HTTP 200, text/event-stream, uncompressed content, and a final [DONE] marker. Headers are limited to 4096 bytes, each HTTP/SSE line to 4095 bytes, decoded text per event to 4095 bytes, and JSON nesting to 16 levels. Only choices[0].delta.content is displayed; role, usage, tools and reasoning fields are ignored. JSON escapes and UTF-8 are validated and converted to CP/M-safe 7-bit text, preserving newline/tab and mapping common smart punctuation; other non-ASCII code points become ?.

The request has a 120-second total deadline, including backpressure. Wi-Fi loss/reconfiguration, premature EOF, allocation/write errors, oversized input, malformed HTTP/JSON and HTTP/provider errors terminate the connection and publish explicit Chat: ... text after already queued content, then EOF. Configuration failures are reported the same way. Diagnostics do not print credentials, prompts, provider error bodies or generated answers. CHATC11 itself has an approximately 30-second no-content timeout and an 8191-byte local answer limit; a long-thinking model can hit that client limit before the firmware deadline. No artificial answer bytes or automatic duplicate POSTs are generated to hide these limits.

Native extended_io_services, chat_http_sse, chat_async_transport and weather_real_tls_config tests exercise the real mailbox/worker/parser/client and both trust roots. They cover chunk framing, split input, full queues, no-duplicate writes, cancellation/restart, failure cleanup, stale callbacks, and missing or invalid configuration. They do not execute the CP/M binary or prove live inference, heap/stack headroom, or combined hardware timing.

docs.title: OpenWeatherMap weather
docs.text:
Phase 10 supports the ESP32 Altair weather ABI through shared service group 0x40 on ports 2/3/4. Do not use the old physical ports 46/47/200: these alias other peripherals on this board.

  • Payload [1] returns one status byte: 0 NONE, 1 FETCHING, 2 READY, or 3 ERROR. Status reads never wait for an HTTP request.
  • Payload [0, field_id] returns length-prefixed text, without a trailing NUL. Units and error text are available before the first successful fetch; other fields return UNAVAILABLE until data exists.
  • Unknown operations, incorrect lengths and unknown fields return the usual explicit service errors. An HTTP failure is exposed by status ERROR and field 12, not by inventing weather data or failing every status query.
Field Text 0 City 1 / 2 Current condition / description 3 / 13 Current temperature / feels-like temperature 4 / 5 Humidity percent / wind speed 6 / 7 Forecast condition / description 8 / 14 Forecast temperature / feels-like temperature 9 First forecast block time, as supplied by OWM in UTC 10 Seconds since the last successful current-data refresh 11 Temperature units: C, F, or K 12 Last error or forecast warning; empty after a fully successful refresh

Temperatures and wind speed are rounded to integer strings as in the reference driver; wind is m/s for metric/standard and mph for imperial. Only the first forecast block is requested (cnt=1).

Configure the existing durable ENV store:

ENV OWM_KEY=<your-api-key>
ENV OWM_LOCATION=Sydney,AU
ENV OWM_UNITS=metric

OWM_KEY is limited to 40 bytes, location to 64 bytes. Location accepts a city/country query or a validated lat=-33.8&lon=151.2 coordinate pair. The ENV CLI treats + and - inside assignments as arithmetic; use its literal insert mode for coordinates or names containing these characters: ENV -D OWM_LOCATION, then ENV -I OWM_LOCATION=lat=-33.8&lon=151.2. Units are metric (default), imperial, or standard. Missing keys or invalid settings produce an explanatory error; no request is sent. Settings are reloaded at most once per second. Changing them cancels an in-flight request, clears data belonging to the old configuration, and starts a new fetch without rebooting. ENV remains plaintext onboard flash; do not publish its contents. Firmware diagnostics never print the key, request URL or provider response body.

Core 1 waits for Wi-Fi and a synchronized SNTP clock, then allows 5 seconds for the network to settle before fetching current conditions and forecast. Successful refreshes repeat every 20 minutes. Initial failures retry every 2 minutes for five retries, then every 20 minutes; failures after a successful fetch use the 20-minute interval. Reconnection schedules a fresh fetch. The last successful cache remains readable after failures, with its increasing age and explicit error status. A failed forecast still publishes valid current conditions as READY, leaves forecast fields empty, and reports a forecast warning in field 12 and on USB.

HTTPS uses port 443, required certificate-chain and hostname verification, and certificate date checks against the SNTP-derived UTC clock. There is no HTTP or insecure-TLS fallback. The bundled USERTrust RSA public root is maintained in weather_ca.pem (SHA-256 E793C9B02FD8AA13E21C31228ACCB08119643B749C898964B1746D46C3D4CBD2, valid through 18 January 2038). Update the trust anchor if the provider changes its chain. Its RSA/SHA-384 signature requires MBEDTLS_SHA384_C; enabling SHA-512 alone does not enable SHA-384 in Mbed TLS 3. Without it, TLS configuration fails while parsing the CA, before DNS or HTTP starts. DNS, connection and response work share a 15-second request deadline; responses are bounded to 16 KiB on the wire and 8 KiB decoded, with at most 2 KiB of HTTP headers. Content-length, connection-close and chunked responses are supported; malformed, oversized or compressed bodies fail explicitly.

The weather worker uses no Z80 trap callbacks, extra core, or blocking socket. Network callbacks only collect bounded data; parsing, ENV access and cache publication happen on core 1 between its normal disk/service/network polls. Phase 10 uses an explicit 8 KiB core-1 stack in main RAM for TLS; Phase 9 retains its original launch path and reports weather UNAVAILABLE.

docs.title: System information and reboot
docs.text: System-info selectors are 0 = hostname z80romless-sbc, 1 = current Wi-Fi IPv4 address, and 2 = Pico unique board ID. The IPv4 selector returns UNAVAILABLE without a connection, including Phase 9. Reboot requires the exact confirmation byte 0xA5; it flushes queued/cached disk writes, then core 0 disables traps, holds reset, isolates the data paths and stops the clock before watchdog reboot. New disk commands are gated before the reboot job is published, with BUSY+ERROR reported on disk status, so writes cannot race the final flush. Failed flushes reopen the gate and report STORAGE_WRITE instead.

docs.title: Onboard LED device
docs.text:
Phases 9 and 10 expose the Pico 2 W onboard LED through Utility group 0x21, using the existing shared-service ports 0x02-0x04. No wiring changes, expansion GPIOs, or additional port IDs are needed; 0x07 remains spare for a future interrupt timer.

  • Payload [4, 0] turns the LED off; [4, 1] turns it on. Success is COMPLETE and requires ACK.
  • Payload [5] returns a one-byte response: 0 off or 1 on. This is the last successfully commanded state, not an optical measurement.
  • Other state values return INVALID_PARAMETER. Incorrect payload lengths return INVALID_LENGTH.
  • An initial read after firmware boot initializes the LED off; an initial write applies the requested state directly. Its state is not persisted to flash, and transport RESET does not undo it.
  • Both phases initialize the wireless-chip driver lazily if necessary. Phase 9 uses the SDK's LED-only pico_cyw43_arch_none backend: no Wi-Fi association or network stack is enabled, and the USB terminal and nominal 20 MHz Z80 operation are unchanged. Phase 10 also works with empty Wi-Fi credentials or without a network connection. Driver initialization/write failures return UNAVAILABLE; a failed write does not update the reported state.

The worker accesses the wireless chip on core 1, never inside the core 0 Z80 I/O trap. LED control is an asynchronous service, not a cycle-timed output.

For example, to turn the LED on, issue these Z80 I/O writes:

OUT port 0x02, value 0x01   ; RESET shared transport
OUT port 0x02, value 0x21   ; Utility group
OUT port 0x03, value 0x02   ; Payload length, low byte
OUT port 0x03, value 0x00   ; Payload length, high byte
OUT port 0x03, value 0x04   ; Set LED operation
OUT port 0x03, value 0x01   ; On (use 0x00 for off)

These are transaction steps, not literal assembly syntax. Poll port 0x02 with a bounded limit until COMPLETE (0x01) or ERROR (0xFF); acknowledge COMPLETE by writing 0x00 to port 0x02. On ERROR, read and acknowledge the framed error as described above. RESET is for recovering/starting an idle channel, not for cancelling another client's active transaction.

docs.title: Persistent environment API
docs.text:
Keys are case-insensitive, stored uppercase, and contain 1-16 non-NUL bytes. Values contain 0-255 non-NUL bytes. Empty and absent values are distinct: GET of an empty value returns a zero-length response; an absent key returns NOT_FOUND.

Operation Payload Result 0 reset / 1 initialize [operation] COMPLETE 2 get [2, key_length_u8, key_bytes] Value text 3 set [3, key_length_u8, key_bytes, value_length_u16, value_bytes] COMPLETE, durable before success 4 delete [4, key_length_u8, key_bytes] COMPLETE or NOT_FOUND 5 list [5] KEY=VALUE lines with CRLF 6 count [6] Decimal count text 7 clear [7] COMPLETE, durable before success 8 exists [8, key_length_u8, key_bytes] COMPLETE or NOT_FOUND 9 execute ENV command [9, command_text], at most 511 command bytes Text

The ENV command parser is shared with the maintained host driver. It supports listing, NAME, NAME=VALUE, copying another variable, numeric addition/ subtraction, NAME+N, NAME-N, -I NAME=VALUE, -D NAME, -N, NOW (uptime seconds), and -H/HELP/?. Numeric overflow is an explicit error. No additional physical ports expose the host's private legacy selectors.

The store supports at most 128 entries, subject to a 3,840-byte serialized snapshot limit. Each entry consumes key length + value length + 2 bytes. There is room for at least 14 maximum-length key/value pairs. Requests that exceed storage or the 2,048-byte reply capacity fail explicitly; LIST never silently truncates. After a failed write, the in-memory state is reloaded from the newest valid durable snapshot; an error does not undo a commit that already reached flash.

Two 4 KiB sectors at 0x2BE000 and 0x2BF000 occupy unused space in the boot partition, beyond the boot payload ending at 0x2B1000. Firmware, the disk journal, boot package and all four disk offsets remain unchanged. Each snapshot has a version, sequence number, payload CRC32 and header CRC32. Updates erase/program the inactive sector, verify the payload, and commit the header last. The previous committed snapshot remains recoverable after an interrupted replacement. A durable empty baseline is established before the first mutation. Repeated unchanged writes do not erase flash.

Flash erase/program uses the disk backend's BUSREQ/BUSACK and flash-safe multicore handshake. A non-success flash-safe result fails closed through watchdog reboot. Both sectors erased means a new empty store; neither erased nor CRC-valid means STORAGE_READ, not a fabricated empty environment. Flash has finite endurance: use countdown timers and stopwatches, not repeated persistent writes, for high-frequency counters.

Preserving environment variables during updates

Firmware-only and exact boot-package-only updates preserve variables. Complete 4 MiB provisioning, mass erase and flash_nuke.uf2 destroy them. Do not write a padded 128 KiB boot-partition image: it would overwrite ENV. Full generated images deliberately contain erased environment sectors.

docs.title: Worked request bytes
docs.text:
These examples show the actual wire framing; prefer the existing dcc svc_operation_send(), svc_get_text() and timer helpers in DXSVC.H. Use bounded client polling, drain error frames, and RESET after failure.

Read uptime:
  OUT 02,20
  OUT 03,01  OUT 03,00       ; payload length = 1
  OUT 03,00                 ; operation = uptime seconds
  IN 02 until 02 or FF       ; RESPONSE_READY or ERROR
  IN 04 twice, then length bytes

Set TZ=UTC0:
  OUT 02,30
  OUT 03,0A  OUT 03,00       ; payload length = 10
  OUT 03,03  OUT 03,02       ; SET, key length
  OUT 03,54  OUT 03,5A       ; "TZ"
  OUT 03,04  OUT 03,00       ; value length = 4
  OUT 03,55  OUT 03,54  OUT 03,43  OUT 03,30  ; "UTC0"
  IN 02 until 01 or FF       ; COMPLETE or ERROR
  OUT 02,00                 ; ACK only after success

docs.title: Independent timer port
docs.text:
Port 0x17 uses no shared-service framing and remains usable while the service worker is BUSY. Its timers/stopwatches are the same instances as groups 0x10/0x11.

OUT command Subsequent transfers 0x00 Reset only this parser; running timers remain unchanged 0x10-0x12 Two OUT bytes, low then high: start millisecond timer 0-2 0x13 One OUT byte: start whole-second timer 3 0x20-0x23 IN returns selected timer's running flag 0x30 IN returns running bitmask, bits 0-3 0x40-0x42 Reset stopwatch 0-2 0x50-0x52 Four IN bytes: latched stopwatch seconds, little-endian 0x60-0x62 Four IN bytes: latched stopwatch milliseconds, little-endian

The parser initially selects the timer bitmask. An invalid command, an IN during parameter collection, or stopwatch over-read returns 0xFF and requires recovery. To recover an unknown state, perform IN 0x17, then OUT 0x17, 0x00. Multi-byte port-23 operations must not be interleaved with other users of that port.

docs.title: Deferred services and validation
docs.text:
File transfer remains reserved on 0x15/0x16; it is not implemented. Chat and Sense HAT requests return explicit UNAVAILABLE errors. Weather is implemented only in Phase 10; Phase 9 reports UNAVAILABLE. The ESP32 interrupt timer on 0x07 is deferred: current hardware has no Pico-to-INT# driver, and the RD#-gated data path cannot provide an interrupt vector. No interrupt, GPIO or PCB wiring changes accompany this work.

Core 0 owns traps and timer state. Core 1 executes slow services after disk service and before network work. A generation-tagged mailbox prevents stale worker replies from becoming new responses. Pause/drain logic accounts for pending service work before flash is declared quiescent. Flash and network work never run inside the I/O trap.

Host tests cover framing, aliases, recovery, timer boundaries and latching, ENV commands/capacity, unchanged-write suppression, snapshot recovery, calendar formatting, phase routing and flash-safe ownership. These are software checks, not bench timing or physical power-cut qualification.

  • Phase 3 owns address wiring.
  • Phase 8 owns initial trap checks.
  • Phase 9 owns flash bring-up.
  • DCC documentation covers port access and CP/M BDOS/BIOS APIs.

docs.title: The three operating states
docs.text:
State Who controls the buses? What you should expect Injected loading Z80 alone drives SRAM addresses and writes RESET# is released after slow reset clocks; Pico supplies instructions with SRAM reads inhibited and verifies CPU-written RAM. Normal execution Z80 addresses SRAM directly Both Pico data paths are isolated; ordinary memory access needs no Pico software. Trapped I/O Z80 holds its address while the Pico services one byte HCT32 WAIT and clock stopping hold the cycle; four buffered address bits select the port.

Runtime flash writes temporarily request the Z80 bus using BUSREQ#/BUSACK#. This is different from cold boot: a running CPU must acknowledge the request before flash programming. The Pico never drives memory addresses or writes, even during a bus grant. The detailed rules below protect that boundary.

docs.title: 6.1 Hardware-WAIT-Assisted Clock-Stop Trap Protocol
docs.text:
IORQ# LOW reaches HCT32 pin 4 and makes WAIT# pin 6 LOW while Pico GP9 IO_RELEASE is LOW. The buffered falling edge interrupts core 0, which stops PWM. The fully static CMOS Z80 tolerates the stopped clock. After settling, firmware first checks that IORQ# remains LOW, then requires exactly one of RD#/WR# active and samples A0/A1/A2/A4 before servicing data. If IORQ# is already HIGH, it counts an inactive interrupt and resumes PWM without touching the data paths or IO_RELEASE. These events remain included in control_errors so they cannot silently pass timing qualification.

For OUT, U10 receives the CPU byte; for IN, U9 supplies a preloaded reply. Only after the path is configured does GP9 rise. Firmware completes the I/O cycle with slow single clocks, observes IORQ/strobe release, disables both paths, waits at least 1 us for isolation, lowers GP9, then restores PWM. Every slow step includes a fixed 1 us LOW settling interval before the control sample, preventing an extra clock caused by propagation or input-synchronizer delay. This prevents a later memory read from re-enabling the Pico output. RD#-qualified U9 OE provides additional strobe gating, not software-independent ownership arbitration.

WAIT assertion is fixed logic, not IRQ/PIO dependent. HCT32 propagation, WAIT setup/hold, PWM-to-SIO transitions, and data setup still require captures. The 500 ms release timeout fails closed through RESET and watchdog recovery.

docs.title: 6.2 Terminal I/O over Pico WebSocket
docs.text:
See I/O ports and services for the overall allocation of fixed terminal/disk ports, reserved diagnostics and proposed extensions.

The final terminal is a virtual I/O peripheral implemented by the Pico, not a Z80-side UART. Z80 software performs ordinary IN and OUT instructions against a small terminal port pair; the Pico intercepts those cycles through the Section 6.1 clock-stop trap, then resumes the CPU after sampling or supplying the data byte. A browser connects to the Pico over Wi-Fi and receives the terminal stream through a WebSocket server running on the Pico 2 W.

Wi-Fi/WebSocket is the intended final and day-one operating terminal. Before networking is introduced, Phase 8 and Phase 9 use USB CDC over the Pico's existing USB connector as an intermediate terminal transport. USB CDC consumes no GPIO and appears as /dev/cu.usbmodem... on macOS. It lets the same 0x00/0x01 virtual-port contract and bounded queues be tested without lwIP timing in the loop. Keep diagnostics framed or on a separate CDC interface so debug text cannot become CP/M input. Those applications uses ordinary bytes as terminal input and reserves Ctrl-] followed by one command byte for framed diagnostics. Phase 10 selects Wi-Fi/WebSocket exclusively while a browser is connected. USB remains the CP/M fallback before connection and after disconnect; framed Ctrl-] diagnostics remain available even while the browser owns CP/M. Network setup uses Ctrl-] n and the existing persistent ENV store.

The WebSocket server must run on the Pico's other core so Wi-Fi, lwIP, HTTP serving, and WebSocket polling cannot interfere with the timing of the Z80-facing supervisor path. Core 0 owns GPIO, clock stop/resume, assisted loading, and the I/O trap. Core 1 owns USB initialization and interrupts, USB console/supervisor parsing, Wi-Fi association, the embedded terminal page, WebSocket accept/send/receive, and network polling. The cores share terminal byte queues, one immutable disk-write queue, a small request/result pair for Z80 bus ownership, and atomic terminal/disk status words; they share no raw bus GPIO ownership. Phase 10 uses the CYW43 polling architecture so network callbacks execute only on core 1. USB commands use a bounded queue to request Z80 actions on core 0; USB never directly changes bus pins. Core 0 publishes CPU state and receives published cancellation/connectivity flags instead of reading USB. All stdout uses a bounded diagnostic ring drained only by core 1. Its default alarm pool is explicitly initialized there, keeping USB background work off core 0. Core 1 starts before journal recovery and participates in flash lockout; runtime workers start only after SRAM verification. Only core 1 reads or writes the runtime ENV backend.

Use the pico-altair-8800 WebSocket console as the software pattern: one embedded HTML terminal page, one WebSocket server, and byte queues between the CPU-facing side and the network-facing side. The trap hook must never call lwIP, print, sleep, wait for a browser, or block on a queue. It may only enqueue Z80 output bytes, dequeue already-buffered browser input bytes, and report terminal status. Core 1 may drop, drain, or back-pressure network data; it must not hold terminal critical sections across network or flash work or touch any Z80 bus GPIO. Pico SDK queue_try_add()/queue_try_remove() do not wait for space or data, but they do use brief internal spinlock critical sections for multicore safety. Include that bounded contention in measured trap-latency qualification rather than describing these queues as lock-free. A short SDK critical section also serializes transmit status, enqueueing and disconnect cleanup so output cannot race with a disconnect on the other core.

The initial terminal decode is intentionally small:

Port Direction Function 0x00 Z80 OUT Terminal transmit byte from Z80 to host terminal 0x00 Z80 IN Terminal receive byte from host to Z80; returns 0x00 if empty 0x01 Z80 IN Terminal status: bit 0 = receive byte available, bit 1 = transmit-ready (queue has room or transport disconnected), bit 7 = transport connected (USB in Phase 9; browser or fallback USB in Phase 10)

Connected terminals retain the 512-byte output buffer. If it is full, a new Z80 output write is discarded and the TX-drop counter increments; older queued characters remain unchanged and in order. The trap never waits for space. Transmit-ready remains clear until space is available, so software that polls it can still wait voluntarily before writing. This policy applies to USB and browser output alike. Without a connected terminal, output writes are discarded immediately and transmit-ready remains set, preventing CP/M console output from waiting for a client. Disconnecting clears queued output; reconnecting does not replay it. These intentional discards do not increment the terminal overflow counter. Phase 10 also clears queued input/output on browser/USB handover and rejects additional browser sessions without changing the active owner. Wi-Fi-only events leave USB-owned queues intact. The Phase 10 browser and firmware use a sequenced, acknowledged binary protocol: up to four 512-byte output frames are retained in flight and cumulatively acknowledged after xterm consumes them. Output survives temporary send failures without duplication. One pending browser input frame waits for RX-queue space and is admitted on the next service pass rather than waiting for retransmission or evicting older bytes. The terminal sends a ping every five minutes. A missing pong is counted at the next five-minute heartbeat; a fifth miss releases the browser to USB. A stalled output ACK still times out after 15 seconds.

This is enough for ROM monitors, BASIC, CP/M console glue, and small diagnostics. If later software needs modem-control style signals, add more virtual status bits before adding hardware.

docs.title: 6.3 Onboard Flash CP/M Disk Storage
docs.text:
The Pico's 4 MiB onboard flash stores its firmware, the Z80 boot package, and four persistent read/write CP/M disks. No external storage, SPI bus, or extra GPIO is required. The linker limits Pico firmware to the first 2.5625 MiB and reserves the remainder as follows:

Region Flash offset Size Contents Journal 0x290000 64 KiB Eight rotating metadata/data sector pairs Boot partition 0x2A0000 128 KiB Header/image through 0x2B0FFF; ENV in final 8 KiB Environment (inside boot partition) 0x2BE000 8 KiB Two alternating CRC-checked 4 KiB snapshots Drive A 0x2C0000 320 KiB CP/M system disk Drive B 0x310000 320 KiB CP/M data disk Drive C 0x360000 320 KiB CP/M data disk Drive D 0x3B0000 320 KiB CP/M data disk

Disk format. Each disk is exactly 327,680 bytes: 80 tracks of 32 sequential 128-byte records. This project-specific format is not IBM 3740 SSSD. Converted Altair source disks are checked into src/disks/generated/, so normal builds need no conversion step. The optional src/disks/convert_altair_disks.py script removes Altair framing and skew, extracts the CP/M records, and pads the images from 77 to 80 tracks.

Build and provisioning. The z80_cpm_images target automatically creates the boot package, four disk images, and combined build/cpm/z80romless-flash.bin. The build does not flash the Pico. For initial setup, put it in BOOTSEL mode and run:

cmake --build build --target z80_cpm_images -j
picotool load -v build/cpm/z80romless-flash.bin -t bin -o 0x10000000
picotool reboot

Use separate artifacts only for selective updates. The firmware build and provisioning page gives their commands and addresses. Full provisioning, flash_nuke.uf2, and mass erase destroy existing disk contents and environment variables, so keep backups.

Phases 9 and 10 implement the ROMLESS-SVC/1 extended I/O protocol, including persistent environment variables. ENV uses the unused boot-partition tail, not the disk journal. Exact firmware-only and boot-package-only updates preserve it; never provision a padded whole-boot-partition image over the ENV sectors.

Runtime behavior. On boot-image initialization, the Pico recovers any interrupted disk update, validates z80boot.pkg, copies its image to Z80 SRAM, and verifies the copy, then resets to PC zero before execution. The BIOS transfers one 128-byte disk record at a time. Core 0 serves reads from memory-mapped flash and queues writes to core 1, which maintains one 4 KiB cache in RP2350 internal SRAM, separate from the Z80's external SRAM. Directory writes flush immediately. Other writes flush on cache eviction, an explicit BIOS request, warm boot, or 250 ms of inactivity.

Phase 9 waits for USB commands rather than automatically executing CP/M: Ctrl+] l loads/verifies with slow injected clocks and holds reset afterward; Ctrl+] g starts at the scope-measured 20 MHz Z80 clock using a 120 MHz supervisor clock. The manifest must describe a complete 65,536-byte image beginning with JP FD00h. BIOS reports on reserved port 0x05 distinguish cold entry (B0h) and CCP handoff (C0h) from the act of releasing reset. A real prompt and filesystem tests remain necessary. The separate Phase 9 automatic-loader target and Phase 10 use automatic verified startup at 20 MHz.

A 64 KiB journal makes 4 KiB sector replacement recoverable after power loss. At startup, firmware replays complete, CRC-valid committed entries and rejects invalid or out-of-range entries. Before erasing a target, it verifies the staged journal data sector and header page by readback; afterward it verifies the complete new target and clears the header. The Phase 9 implementation guide defines the journal sequence, multicore lockout, failure handling, and tests.

Flash has finite erase endurance. The cache coalesces writes and skips clean blocks, but sustained write-heavy workloads should use replaceable or wear-levelled storage.

docs.title: 6.4 System Performance Envelope & Constraints
docs.text:
• I/O Decode Width: Four buffered lines A0/A1/A2/A4, mask 0x17. A3/A5-A7 and the high byte alias; terminal 00/01 and disk 10-14 remain distinct.

  • Trap Latency Profile: HCT32-generated WAIT# covers the interval from IORQ# falling until IO_RELEASE reports a configured data path. The Pico stops the static CPU clock while servicing the cycle. Measure IORQ#-to-WAIT#, WAIT# setup/hold, the final PWM edge, and IO_RELEASE-to-WAIT# release and stepped completion at every claimed rate. The design remains suitable for low-rate virtual peripherals, not high-speed line tracing.

  • Clock Validation Targets:

  • Bring-Up Target: 1 MHz, qualified only after a logic-analyzer capture proves every I/O cycle stops before the Z80 samples or releases its data.

  • Qualification Range: 2 MHz – 6 MHz, tested in the increments in the frequency-qualification plan. No rate in this range is guaranteed in advance.

  • Experimental Range: Requests 6.5 MHz – 8 MHz may be attempted in requested 500 kHz steps only after 6 MHz passes. At 144 MHz clk_sys, the 6.5 MHz request still produces 6 MHz; subsequent requests produce approximately 6.545455, 7.2, and exactly 8 MHz nominally. These rates are exploratory, not design claims, because the 55 ns SRAM and breadboard margin dominate despite the faster buffer.

  • Failure Boundary: Any WAIT setup/hold failure, SRAM setup failure, malformed clock edge, or repeatable memory/I/O error ends qualification at the preceding passing step.

  • 20 MHz CPU Rating: The Z84C0020PEC rating applies to the CPU, not this breadboard system with no memory wait states. At 20 MHz a clock period is 50 ns, shorter than the SRAM's 55 ns rated access time even before AHCT244/HCT32 propagation, Z80 setup, and breadboard delay. Reaching 20 MHz requires a redesigned control path, hardware-generated memory and I/O wait states (or deterministic clock gating), and a PCB-level signal- integrity review; changing the Pico PWM frequency is insufficient.

  • PCB Deferred: The existing layout implements the previous circuit. It provides no qualification evidence or manufacturing package for this assisted-loader revision.

docs.title: Pico build, flashing, and USB tools
docs.text: Run these tools from the Z80ROMlessSBC project folder. Use the VS Code tasks for routine builds and deployment; use the scripts directly for device selection or diagnostics.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
Follow Toolchain for the complete Arm GNU toolchain, Pico SDK, Python 3.11+, and picotool. Flashing uses macOS/Linux shell tools (lsof and ps) and a Python environment:

python3 -m venv .venv-flash
.venv-flash/bin/python -m pip install -r scripts/requirements-flash.txt

Before flashing

Save CP/M work and finish any running hardware test. Apply external +5 V before USB and keep it applied. Disk updates overwrite selected drives without backups.

docs.title: VS Code build and firmware tasks
docs.text:
Open the Command Palette, choose Tasks: Run Task, then select:

Exact task name Action Build and flash Pico - Phase 9 firmware Select diagnostic or automatic loader; preserves disks and ENV Build and flash Pico - Phase 9 firmware and disks Select variant; replaces complete flash image, including disks and ENV Flash Pico - Phase 6 20 MHz scope diagnostic Builds and force-flashes the isolated CPU/SRAM scope diagnostic Build and flash Pico - Phase 10 firmware Builds and force-flashes firmware; preserves disks and ENV Prepare interactive CP/M emulator Builds the host emulator, I/O adapter, and CP/M images; no Pico required

Phase 9 and 10 firmware tasks build and deploy. They force-update without a previous-firmware handshake, verify written bytes, and request reboot while preserving disks and ENV. Save work before using them. Phase 9 tasks prompt for Diagnostic (bring-up) or Automatic loader (normal operation after tests pass).

For a new board or coordinated BIOS/boot-package changes, follow Firmware build and provisioning. Use the Phase 9 and Phase 10 guides in bring-up order.

docs.title: Deployment task requirements
docs.text:
Build/flash pairs are available for Phases 1–6 and 8, including optional Phase 6 memory screens and soak tests. Each phase page lists its exact tasks. Phase 0 has no firmware.

  • Build Pico - … builds only.
  • Flash Pico - … tasks build, force BOOTSEL entry, verify firmware, and reboot without checking or handshaking with the previous phase firmware.
  • Save work before flashing and follow each phase's power/device requirements. Initial Phase 1 programming uses the Pico off the breadboard.
  • If firmware cannot respond to picotool's USB boot request, enter BOOTSEL manually. This does not require a particular previous phase.

docs.title: Firmware and disks
docs.text: The Build and flash Pico - Phase 9 firmware and disks task builds and writes the complete flash image. It replaces firmware, boot package, disks, journal, and ENV without backups. It requires USB serial selection and explicit confirmation, and forces BOOTSEL entry without a firmware handshake. Use firmware-only tasks to preserve existing disks and settings.

docs.title: VS Code disk flashing tasks
docs.text:
Choose Tasks: Run Task, then one of:

Exact task name Source in src/disks/source-altair/ Flash Pico - All disks (A-D) All four sources below Flash Pico - Drive A cpm63k.dsk Flash Pico - Drive B bdsc-v1.60.dsk Flash Pico - Drive C escape-posix.dsk Flash Pico - Drive D blank.dsk
  • Select Replace selected disks at the confirmation prompt.
  • A: is regenerated with native CP/M system tracks and AUTORUN.COM under build/cpm-disk-update/; this requires z80asm and cpmtools.
  • B:–D: are validated and converted at flash time.
  • Tasks force BOOTSEL entry without a firmware handshake, check the journal, verify selected writes, and reboot once. They preserve firmware, the boot package, ENV, and unselected drives.
  • A: must match the installed boot package; an incompatibility aborts the update.

These tasks do not compile applications. Update the source disk first; see Related projects for building and importing apps.

docs.title: Maintained scripts
docs.text:
Script Purpose scripts/pico_build.py Finds a complete Arm GNU/Newlib toolchain, configures CMake, and builds the requested target scripts/pico_flash.py Verified firmware/disk writes, BOOTSEL preparation, and journal checks scripts/pico_supervisor.py Serial discovery, status, help, clean stop, and optional boot checks src/disks/convert_altair_disks.py Converts validated Altair disk images to native images src/cpm/build_images.py Builds board-native CP/M disks, boot packages, and optional complete flash images

Use --help for current options. For example:

python3 scripts/pico_build.py --build-dir build --target z80_stage09_flash_storage
.venv-flash/bin/python scripts/pico_supervisor.py ports
.venv-flash/bin/python scripts/pico_flash.py --help

docs.title: Firmware updates
docs.text:
For a matching, already provisioned installation:

.venv-flash/bin/python scripts/pico_flash.py firmware \
  build/src/stage09_flash_storage/z80_stage09_flash_storage.uf2 \
  --power-confirmed

The CLI normally disconnects picocom and requests a clean stop/flush before flashing. --force skips that handshake for firmware and disk updates, as the VS Code deployment tasks do. Unknown serial owners or failed verification abort the update.

Firmware writes must stay below flash offset 0x290000. They preserve disks and boot data. Verification confirms written bytes, not a successful CP/M boot; check operation separately using the phase guide.

docs.title: Selective disk updates without backups
docs.text:
For custom disk assignments:

.venv-flash/bin/python scripts/pico_flash.py disks \
  --drive B=src/disks/source-altair/bdsc-v1.60.dsk \
  --drive C=src/disks/source-altair/escape-posix.dsk \
  --power-confirmed

Repeat --drive DRIVE=IMAGE for unique A:–D: slots. Native images must be 327,680 bytes. Altair images are accepted for B:–D:; A: requires a prepared native image matching the installed boot package. The VS Code A: task handles that preparation automatically.

A pending journal or failed verification stops the update. Multiple-drive writes are not atomic; earlier drives may already be replaced if a later write fails.

docs.title: Device selection and diagnostics
docs.text:
The tools select a unique Pico automatically. Run pico_supervisor.py ports to list devices; use --serial DEVICE_SERIAL when several are connected. Standalone supervisor commands require the serial terminal to be closed.

Command after scripts/pico_supervisor.py Purpose ports List serial devices without opening them status Read supervisor status help Read the running firmware's command menu stop Stop/flush CP/M and confirm clean storage wait-boot Await a fresh CP/M prompt and check status; does not reset

The supervisor uses the Phase 9-style USB protocol implemented by the running firmware. For other bring-up firmware, follow its phase instructions.

Additional pico_flash.py options:

Option or command Purpose --port PORT Restrict serial-port discovery --no-disconnect Refuse a busy port instead of closing picocom --stopped Skip stop/flush after an operator-confirmed clean stop --bootsel --stopped --serial DEVICE_SERIAL Select a device already in BOOTSEL --no-reboot Leave BOOTSEL after firmware/disk writes prepare --power-confirmed Stop/flush, enter BOOTSEL, and check the journal without writing journal --serial DEVICE_SERIAL Read-check journal headers on a device already in BOOTSEL

prepare changes device state; it is not a passive status query. Investigate a failed stop or pending journal rather than bypassing it.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
• Missing serial: install scripts/requirements-flash.txt in .venv-flash.
  • No unique Pico: list ports and select the intended USB serial number.
  • Busy port: close the terminal; flashing can close picocom, but not unknown owners.
  • Failed stop or write: retain the output and investigate before retrying.

For host-only script checks:

.venv-flash/bin/python -m unittest discover -s scripts -p 'test_pico*.py' -v
.venv-flash/bin/python -m unittest discover -s src/disks -p 'test_*.py' -v
